title: Ask HN: How to deal with shipping AI-written code you don't understand?
author: rzk
story_text: I saw this LinkedIn post from a Meta engineer and it resonated with me:  https://www.linkedin.com/posts/ali-hamie_im-an-engineer-at-m...  > I'm an engineer at Meta and I never felt this uncomfortable doing my job. I'm writing code these days and it all feels like a black box. This new standard of shipping with AI is moving so fast that if we're going to spend our time checking each line of code, it's going to take forever. That means you can end up with systems you've built where you don't truly understand how all the code works. You understand the high level, but not every detail. And maybe this is becoming the new standard. It goes against every instinct of being a software engineer. I'm used to understanding what I'm building. Now I'm trying to figure out how much I need to understand before I'm comfortable moving forward. Are other engineers feeling this too? How are you handling this?

title: Launch HN: Agent37 (YC F26) – Low-cost agent sandboxes for running agents
author: vishnukool
story_text: Hey HN, I’m Vishnu from Agent37 ( https://agent37.com ). We build sandboxes for running AI agents at under 10% of the cost of most sandbox providers. Our customers spend an average of $0.37/month per sandbox. You can view a video walkthrough of the product here:  https://youtu.be/DK5ISR2tbNo  We started as one of those OpenClaw wrapper companies back in February (yup.. judge me). In time we added more and more harnesses. One of the goals I had at the time was to offer a free plan to users, so as to gain more market share. But it was too cost prohibitive to do it right away. Especially since we were bootstrapped and servers were running on my savings. Today we’re actually able to offer the free plan thanks to the optimizations we’ve made since. Over 90% of the new signups we have are just free plan users and they host their personal Hermes/Openclaw/Claude Code etc on our cloud. Our infrastructure cost for the free sandboxes averages around $0.05 to $0.10 per user per month. Here are some techniques that have worked for lowering cost: * When you look at agent harnesses, they have certain patterns in the way they consume CPU and RAM. They need CPU in bursts when they’re initializing or performing certain tasks, but beyond that, they’re often not peaking. They need more RAM for things like browser and computer-use tasks. Once the task is done, usage often comes back down. This is a key insight in lowering cost, so by efficiently managing the CPU/RAM utilization we could lower the cost. * Secondly, you have to skip the hyperscalers when renting the Hosts. I worked at Amazon before and they have 80-90% margins on VMs. So it was an obvious choice once I looked at the prices to go one layer down to vendors like Hetzner and OVH. This alone was probably one of the biggest cost levers in reducing the cost. * Thirdly, you also want to pick a technology stack that lets you efficiently cache and share resources across the host. We use gVisor for better utilization and fast boot times. It lets us use available host memory across sandboxes without reserving a full VM’s memory for each one. There are tradeoffs: our gVisor sandboxes don’t support workloads like Docker-in-Docker or Android emulators. * And finally the size and shape of the hosts you buy also makes a big difference. RAM is typically the bottleneck when it comes to cost and not the CPU. This is specifically true for agent harness workloads, so when buying servers, we optimize for packing more RAM into a given host. We also host full VM sandboxes for workloads that need them, including running Docker at a slightly higher price, but they are still pretty low cost given the rest of the techniques. Overall, my learning has been that just by focusing on a niche of sandbox usecases, and optimizing for it you can give a much better cost/performance tradeoff. I was previously a Senior Software Engineer at Amazon and an Engineering Manager at Quantcast. I built Amazon's internal AI chatbot, Diya, and their internal coding harness, Ziya. If you’re someone who’s looking to run agents on sandbox and are exploring a sandbox vendor, come check us out. We’re particularly looking for developers building messaging agents to try their workloads and challenge the limits and economics of our platform. Thanks!  https://agent37.com

title: Maxwell: A new kind of model that sits between code and hardware
author: laginimaineb
story_text: Hi HN, I'm Gal from doubleAI. We've built Maxwell, a new kind of frontier model we call a Code Execution Model. It sits between your code and the hardware. No humans in the loop! Maxwell makes the code run faster as it runs, without ever changing a single line. Maxwell sees programs from the inside: traces, profiling information, and the data flowing through them. It adapts dynamically to the environment, including the hardware, what else is running, and what the inputs look like. Code execution models change the way we approach coding. Today, Claude/Codex (and humans) keep re-optimising code for every different use-case hardware and data flow (think of LLM inference engines, like vLLM!). Our bet is that this is unnecessary, suboptimal, and that it does not scale. Instead, we think the right answer is to make code a living, thinking, thing. Early access is open at heymaxwell.ai. Happy to answer questions here.

title: Show HN: Omnara – Open-source alternative to Claude Managed Agents
author: kmansm27
story_text: Hey all, Kartik from Omnara ( https://omnara.com ) here. We're building an open-source API for running durable agents. You create an agent with an API call, and Omnara runs the agent loop, gives the agent sandboxes to run commands in, and handles secrets, permissions, and RBAC. Each agent's state is stored in Postgres, so agents survive restarts and cost nothing while idle. You can message them and stream their events over the API. You may remember us from our early days, when we made a remote-control phone app for Claude Code and Codex. Since the harness ran on a laptop back then, we had to build a relay to reach it, it stopped when the laptop closed, and moving it to a cloud sandbox meant syncing code and agent state between machines. We didn't think remote-controlling a local agent was end-game for how people would run agents, so we built a new product where the agent runs in the cloud, any client can talk to it through an API, and it can still use your laptop as one of its machines. Anthropic and OpenAI are building hosted versions of this, like Claude Managed Agents and the OpenAI Agents API. Omnara is an open-source version you can run on your own servers and use your own models. It's basically a harness server like the opencode or codex servers, but durable, scalable, with the usual harness features like file and shell tools, subagents, compaction, permission prompts, MCP, skills, memory, yada yada yada. Here's some interesting architectural decisions we made while building this out: Most harnesses, like Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi, Goose, etc, run the agent loop in one long-lived process that keeps its log in a JSONL or SQLite file. In Omnara, the log is an append-only event log in Postgres, with inputs, model outputs and tool calls stored as typed rows in their own tables. The loop runs on stateless workers in the control plane. A worker runs one iteration of the loop, either a model call or the tool calls it produced, then releases the agent and puts the next iteration on a queue in Postgres. Whichever worker is free picks it up, so each iteration of an agent's loop can run in a different process on a different machine. Each iteration's result commits in one transaction, so the model output, its tool calls, usage and the next wakeup are saved together or not at all. If a worker dies mid-iteration, nothing commits, its lease expires, and another worker retries it. Agents waiting on a user, a tool or a retry don't hold a worker, so one worker can multiplex thousands of agents. Also unlike other harnesses, the machines that the workers (our agent loop) run on aren't where the agent runs its commands. Instead, any macOS or Linux machine with an internet connection, like your laptop or any cloud sandbox, can run a small daemon (omnarad) that connects out to Omnara, so it doesn't need any open inbound ports. The agent then gets tools for that machine, like running a command or editing a file. An agent can have any number of machines connected to it. A fun thing I like to do is I have my laptop and a cloud sandbox connected to the same agent, so when my laptop is on, my agent codes there and I can interact with it, and I have it often push to Github. When I close my laptop, my agent sees the laptop went offline, pulls the latest changes to its cloud sandbox, and continues there. The entire codebase is open source at  https://github.com/omnara-ai/omnara , and it’s self hostable, even on a single machine with docker compose. You can also use the hosted version at  https://omnara.com . Let me know what you think!

title: Show HN: Spotatui, a Spotify TUI/GUI without web API rate limits
author: LargeModGames
story_text:
About 11 months ago i revived the amazing but unfortunately unmaintained spotify-tui. Since then I have been working on it almost non stop, finding a lot of problems on the way. One of the main issues I ran into were the Spotify web API rate limits. Third party clients like spotatui are dependent on a developer app made in the Spotify developer dashboard, which get rate limited a lot and Spotify has slowly been deprecating endpoints from it. The workaround for this used to be using a shared client id from ncspot but unfortunately that got rate limited too. This is when i started adding other playback sources, including YouTube, Navidrome/Subsonic, Internet radio with +- 30.000 stations, local files, Qobuz for lossless audio and Apple Music for macOS only where it controls the music app remotely. I fixed both the deprecated endpoints and the rate limits with one solution. It still uses librespot in the back, my spotatui specific fork, but gets all data from it instead of only playback. The data comes from the internal API of the official clients, that API gives metadata, playlists, the user library, devices, lyrics and audio analysis. For searching it uses Pathfinder, the internal GraphQL API. There are no web API rate limits because there is no shared app quota. Every user uses their own session as if it was the official client. The only potential problem is that Spotify does not document this API so any change on their side would break it. I intend to fix any of those issues as soon as they pop up. It all started as a TUI back in 2019 but since then I've added a GUI to it too. The GUI is still a bit behind the TUI in terms of features, it only ships Spotify for now, but full parity between the TUI and GUI is coming soon. After that full parity with the official client is next. That is also why I made the GUI looks almost the same as the official client. That way its easier for me and users to find missing features. Spotatui also has lua scripting support, a optional Web companion on spotatui.com, and if you have a AI coding agent like ChatGPT codex or Claude Code you can enable the MCP tools, which lets AI become your personal DJ just by talking to it. Its written in Rust, uses ratatui for the terminal UI and Tauri 2 for the GUI. The Rust core starts a small web server with localhost that only your pc can reach which the GUI then serves. Both frontends share the same playback logic, the same login and the same Spotify code. The only difference is how you interact with it. On first launch it opens a web browser where you need to login with your Spotify premium account (premium is not optional), that is the whole setup done. I would love any feedback about bugs you encounter or features you would like to see.
GitHub:  https://github.com/LargeModGames/spotatui 
Releases:  https://github.com/LargeModGames/spotatui/releases/latest 
Website:  https://spotatui.com/  Thanks to librespot for making this all possible

title: Anthropic Console overcharged my card 100x due to internationalization input bug
author: rsorto
story_text:
I am a LegalTech Attorney leading a developer team from Costa Rica. While trying to load credits onto my Anthropic API account (claude.com), I experienced a critical internationalization (i18n) and UX failure that has placed an unfair financial burden on me due to a severe oversight in their payment pipeline. The platform prompted me for a payment. Since I am in a Spanish-speaking region where localized systems and keyboards handle dots and commas differently, I typed 5.04. Anthropic’s input system completely failed to sanitize or validate the data. Instead of throwing a formatting error or converting it properly, it silently stripped the decimal internally and instantly charged my credit card $504.00 USD instead of $5.04 USD. To make matters worse, there was no confirmation modal or review screen summarizing the final amount before processing the transaction. It was a single-click, instantaneous overcharge. Anticipating the Obvious Skepticism:
Before anyone suggests "you should have checked your regional settings" or "just wait for the chargeback": 1. Users are not the QA team: In financial software, a system is never supposed to guess or automatically manipulate a numerical input without explicit validation. If an input is ambiguous due to locale differences, the application must reject it or ask for clarification, not execute a 100x overcharge. 2. Scale of the vulnerability: This time it was $504.00, which is an unfair and frustrating burden for independent developers. But because this pipeline completely lacks a confirmation screen and basic input sanitization, the exact same bug could happen to someone typing 50.00 and end up charging them $5,000.00 or more instantly. It is a systemic financial risk. 3. The Chargeback Illusion: Yes, I have already initiated a chargeback with my bank in Costa Rica. However, banking processes here are slow and take up to 120 days to resolve. In the meantime, the $504.00 has already been deducted and charged to my credit card statement. I am forced to pay for Anthropic’s engineering mistake out of my own pocket right now. The Support Wall:
I filed an official complaint on the exact same day, minutes after it happened. I wasn't met with a human; I was blocked by an automated support BOT. The bot repeatedly and rigidly denied the refund, closing the ticket by citing generic policies without a single human ever looking at the fact that the overcharge was caused by a technical bug in their own platform. As developers, we build systems that process people's money. Omitting a confirmation screen on a financial transaction, failing to sanitize localized numerical inputs, and then hiding behind unyielding AI support bots to keep money that doesn't belong to you is completely unacceptable. If anyone from Anthropic's billing or engineering team is reading this, please look into this bug and review my case. It is a critical flaw that is actively harming international developers who are just trying to build on your ecosystem. Pura vida! R.S.G.

title: Show HN: Parsimony – an open-source benchmark for how much code AI models add
author: lasu
story_text: Existing benchmarks measure solve rate and token output/cost, but don't punish excess code, which makes a codebase harder to work with in the long term. I wanted to measure this since it matters most for long-term projects. Method: it takes the patches that benchmarks already publish (DeepSWE, SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Live) and counts "coding units": syntax elements like statements, calls, names and literals. I didn't use lines of code, so cramming code isn't rewarded. Deleted code is subtracted, so it measures net units. GPT-6 and Claude 5.5 have no public patches yet, so I ran them myself on 3–10 tasks on my own subscriptions (shown as faded circles, not ranked). Any feedback or model contributions are welcome, especially public patch exports for newer models. GitHub:  https://github.com/La5u/Parsimony  Not affiliated with any of the benchmarks.

title: Show HN: Agent.reviews – Where AI agents read and write reviews on tools
author: screm
story_text:
Hi HN! I’m Louis, Co-Founder of Armature (YC P26), where we help teams make their product discoverable and usable by coding agents. We already measured 50k+ agent sessions and realized that over and over agents would encounter the exact same limitations on different tasks using the same tool. So we wondered why these weren’t fixed. And the answer is simple: the feedback loop just doesn’t exist between agents and software vendors but also between different agents. Humans can share their experience on platforms like  https://g2.com  and  https://trustpilot.com , but agents have nowhere to. So we created:  https://agent.reviews : the G2 for agents. It works with a set of skills and an npm CLI (@armature-tech/agent-reviews) connecting agents to our API endpoints. Anyone can ask their agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, etc.) to install it, and agents will naturally check reviews before picking a tool and post their own after using one. As usual, privacy was our main concern, so we added 3 layers before a review gets posted:
Deterministic rules filtering secrets, PII, URLs, etc.
A Jev classifier trained to detect any leak after the first check
A small LLM checking each review to make sure nothing was missed We've been sharing this project around for a few weeks now and gathered thousands of reviews already. There are already interesting ones, for example: - A Claude Code agent noticed that the Stripe SDK systematically crashed when the API key was missing on the health check page (while it’s this page’s role to actually return an “API key missing” error) - 2 agents mentioned that Prisma required a DATABASE_URL variable even when it wasn’t connecting to any database. They both put fake URLs as a workaround, and it worked. We truly think the agent experience needs the same community effect user experience has, so everyone benefits from it: agents can pick the tools that are best optimized for them and software companies can improve their product based on real feedback. That’s why we made sure accessing reviews is free for both humans and agents and just requires copy/pasting one prompt for the agent to install our CLI & skill, start the authentication flow, and submit their first review (this helps us prevent unauthorized scraping and spam reviews). Would you let your agents submit and read reviews too?
We’d love for you to set up agent reviews, ask your agent to check reviews next time it needs to pick a tool and post its own experience when using it. Then tell us how it went!

title: Launch HN: Alter (YC S25) – Access control for multi-user agents
author: simfinii
story_text:
Hi HN! We’re Srikar and Kevan, founders of Alter –  https://alterauth.com/ . We’re building access control for agents that can take actions on behalf of multiple users. If you’ve built an internal agent people use through Slack, you may have experienced this scenario: everyone signs in with their own account, but the agent connects to the CRM or billing system with one shared API key, so the agent can do anything that the key can do. User-level authentication in Slack does nothing to control what the agent can do in an external system like the CRM or billing system. Here’s what Alter does: -It acts as a proxy and manages downstream credentials for every API request that an agent takes; -It takes identity into account for every action the agent does. Automatically take into account the end user identity of the person that the agent is taking actions on behalf of. -It enforces fine grained runtime policies and records compliance grade audit logs. Here’s a demo video:  https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9ZqPU14ipGE  We started this because we saw first hand how hard it is to build agents in regulated industries. To unlock the true benefits of agents we need to allow agents to take actions, sometimes actions on behalf of end users. I (Srikar) was working at Goldmans and I saw how prohibitively expensive it was for me as a developer to write my own custom auth to enable multi-tenancy in agents and to allow agents to have strict policy controls as they act on behalf of end users. My co-founder, Kevan, is a second time founder and was previously working on a database startup. He has experience building and selling deep tech into highly regulated environments. So this problem seemed like a natural fit for the both of us. Building and maintaining custom auth for multi tenant agents was challenging. But so was ensuring that the solution we developed was secure, scalable and keeping track of security grade audit logs. As a result we realized there needs to be a separate product category for this that enables developers to easily build secure multi user agents that can actually take actions in an enterprise.
Some of the real-world use cases we’ve seen include: We have built a multi user open claw for our own team using Alter that saved us countless hours on our GTM effort.  Link here: https://github.com/AlterAIDev/openclaw-alter-plugin  We have multiple startups who have used our platform to build their own secure internal agents for everything ranging from SRE agents to back office agents dealing with Quickbooks and payroll platforms like Rippling. It has saved developers countless hours both in terms of building and maintenance. We also have a defense contractor building air gapped agents for marine corp using Alter. Under the hood, the value that we provide is that we do a lot of the plumbing that no one wants to do. We support hundreds of providers, all manually tested end to end. Reliability is our biggest priority. We have built this in a way to allow developers to custom build their agents however they see fit. Everything ranging from custom policies, agent delegation, user attribution, audit logs needed for compliance to a LLM gateway with guardrails (Coming soon) Building a security product is hard. We have learnt that in order to build a truly secure product, security thinking has to pervade every part of the development process. We have embraced shift left security. Every PR that is pushed out is continuously checked for supply chain attacks, potentially dangerous code patterns etc. Our business plan revolved around usage based pricing. There is a free tier up to 10k requests and then a pricing tier starting beyond that. We would love it if people configured their APIs and OAuth credentials, tried out the policies and actually built agents that can take actions with alter! If you’ve built an agent that acts for multiple users, how are you handling permissions today? We’d especially like to hear what you’ve had to build yourself.  https://alterauth.com/

title: Show HN: ADRs for AI – Deliberation records for human–AI work, versioned in Git
author: lumbroso
story_text: Why is this worth your time? Essentially, this solves two problems of AI-assisted programming: (a) the first problem is how to do  oversight  and  what  do oversight  of  and this is solved through the ORRCF (for  Options, Recommendation, Rationale, Confidence, Falsifier) question format (in which models are supposed to surface all their doubts with fully fleshed out recommendations, with falsifier, to be approved or overridden) (b) the second problem is how to scaffold sustainable AI-written code; the ADRs (Architectural Deliberation Records, after Nygard's decision records) written by the models, summarize all the thought process involved in any design decision and provides the blueprint for the code. In tandem, the records provide both the reason why certain non-obvious design choices were made, from a constant, to a library choice, to an ordering in an operation; and also under what conditions different decisions would be made, for instance, in a different platform, or under different latency requirements, or for a different audience, and so on. This is a framework I've been working for over a year, that is the starting point of all my projects. It involves a lot of moving parts and my challenge is figuring out onboarding. I'm hoping the plugin, ADRs4AI/plugins, just created and now also submitted to Anthropic's marketplace, will make it easier. I am also in the process of recording introductory videos. story_text: I'm a software engineer from the east coast (who has lived in Boston, NY, the bay area, UK, France), and I built a task system called 3 & Done.  It's the place you trust to store everything you need to do.  It accepts voice input for rapid entry, as well as text (it stores the audio locally so you can listen to jog your memory) and emails you every morning with the three most important things for you to do that day, and why, based on what you've said about the task: deadlines, urgency, sitting too long. I've been at software engineering for about 44 years now... Grew up with it, which was unusual when I started, and I was always good about getting into the zone and doing things.  The career started small, small company, then back office, the dot com startups, then smaller companies again after the bust, a non-profit, and eventually YouTube (Google at the time, but just barely) and Meta (just Facebook when I was there). When I hit the startups, and later big tech, it was no longer enough to just be an engineer, to have drive, to be good, you had to be organized, you had to follow through, get stuff done, and that's where the task systems started. Twenty-five over the years (and yes, I've actually counted), from Moleskine notebooks with Getting Things Done, evernote (remember evernote?), bug trackers, todoist, asana, google keep, among others. When I managed on the Facebook News Feed, I got into gantt charts (for me and my team), spreadsheets, OmniPlan... I remember apologizing to my director for being so disorganized (because I felt I was making a mess of it), and he told me that I was the most organized engineer he knew. That was because I was doing all of the work in the background, the trimming, the sorting, the reviews, but it was just so much work.  Which was why I changed from system to system.  Each time it built up, and I had to spend more time looking at things I couldn't or didn't get done, when I was rushed and couldn't put time into today's review, it would pile up, and then using it was so much work that I would start taking mini-notes, just emailing myself a few things to do the next day. That's actually the thesis of the app (but not where it started), that if I could just have a few things to do emailed to me each day, I could get it done. This app actually started when I described my previous startup failures into a Claude web session, and it repeated back to me what I had just said.  My previous failures were because I spent too much time building the stuff I needed, and not building what I was supposed to be building. I decided that the app would email me three things to do every day (which matches best practices for attention), but that the day was always yours to decide.  We won't overload you, but you can add more, if you're feeling up to it, or cut back, and we never shame and try our best not to nag (I often only finish two).  If we get it wrong, you can tell us, and we'll re-rank it once a day, or you can set it manually, and if you do, we never override that choice.  The web app is live, and native for both platforms is coming.  In the meantime, on Android, you can use gestures to quick launch into the voice input so saving a task is only a gesture away (e.g. double-tap the back of a Pixel, double-press the power button on Motorola). Now let's talk about the dirty parts.  I used AI to help me build this. Anthropic models mostly, and the brains of the app come from Anthropic models (I like the quality, I like the privacy, absolutely no training on customer data, and the stance of the company).  This app is not some one-shot wonder where I asked frontier models to build a task system and then I put it on a server to show you. I have prompts for the various features (e.g. ranking, generating suggestions, task extractions), I have eval sets of task lists (not anyone's real tasks, but constructed from patterns in my tasks, or the tasks of testers who allowed me to fix the problems they were having), with the three I expect to come out. I store the eval outputs, and re-test whenever I add a new rule to a prompt, or whenever testing a new model version.  The great thing about having this eval set is that it catches when I get it wrong.  When I introspect a failed run, sometimes it's because I need to tune a prompt, but sometimes it's because I missed something in my own ranking. I did the same thing with my infrastructure as well, so this time, instead of setting up servers, and building login systems, and managing databases, I built on Vercel (git push to serving Next.js), Neon (hosted postgres). I started getting emails mailed to me by mid-June, but started getting usable suggestions on June 26, and I've been using it every morning since.  I wanted it to be easy to get started, and easy to use, so the input handles mess (you can add multiple tasks in the same run-on sentence, and a friend who helped me test it just pasted his entire obsidian todo list in wholesale to get started). I wanted to make sure that anyone could try it out, so I built a trial feature that uses the real in-app ranking with a list of items you provide. If you want to try the service, there's a free 14-day trial (card required), and then it's $99/year or $9.99/month after that (plus sales tax).  We warn you seven days before your card is charged and if you cancel, you keep access through the term (either the trial, or our last paid period).  Online, through settings -> billing, no email, no call. I really hope you'll try it out.  If you do, please tell me if we did a good job picking out your day.  https://3anddoneapp.com/try

title: Launch HN: Respan (YC W24) – Open-source Rust AI gateway built around plugins
author: Andydy25
story_text: Hey HN, this is Andy from Respan ( https://www.respan.ai ). We are building an open-source Rust AI gateway. It is a decoupled gateway, so everything is a plugin, including different providers, protocols (MCP, voice), modalities (images, videos), and gateway features (fallbacks, PII redaction, smart routing). Instead of packaging tons of providers and features into one gateway, Respan provides a small core and public interfaces that teams can use to assemble the AI infrastructure their application needs. That way, users can build their own features as additional plugins without having to change the gateway's core. Here’s a video demo:  https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pVv2ibXiTXM  There are countless LLM gateways and most of them solve a common problem: calling different providers from a single endpoint. However, adding new features can become prohibitively difficult. So developers can end up building another gateway to solve a specific problem. We've been building our gateway based on LiteLLM since 2024, and now it's providing services for thousands of orgs. Each org needs different API key settings, routes, and limits. To support that, we kept wrapping LiteLLM, adding more features to it, and at one stage, our wrapper code exceeded 100,000 lines. This January, a routine LiteLLM upgrade caused intermittent connection errors, and we had to roll back. We still haven't figured out the cause, but since then, we no longer upgrade LiteLLM directly and instead manually backport upstream fixes. These experiences made us realize that continuing to patch LiteLLM is not a sustainable long-term solution, and we had to redesign the gateway ourselves. While redesigning our gateway, we wanted to make it easier to add features without breaking existing ones. Inspired by Nginx, we think an AI gateway should have a really small core, only responsible for dispatching events. We believe that everything should be a plugin in our gateway, including providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini), protocols (chat, realtime voice, MCP), modalities (images, videos), and gateway features for reliability and security (smart routing, fallbacks, and PII redaction through example plugins). Beyond that, we want developers to be able to easily extend the gateway's capabilities by adding their own plugins, without touching the core. Adding a provider, even your own, is dead simple, because quirks are plugins too and there’s nothing magical about them. A provider is a short file, Mistral’s is 22 lines, and each quirk, like Groq putting token usage in its own field, gets its own test. Respan Gateway does more than let you call Claude or Gemini models from the OpenAI SDK. It handles tools, images, and reasoning protocols automatically: an application based on the OpenAI Realtime API can also use Gemini Live through the gateway, though not every feature translates. A simple chat app can use MCP tools configured in the gateway, without implementing MCP itself. We also parse requests into a shared structure. When the client and provider use the same API, we preserve provider-specific fields in their native format, even if our shared structure doesn't have a field for them. That way, the gateway can write them back instead of dropping them. Here’s how it works: An adapter hands each HTTP or WebSocket connection to the first client format that recognizes it. The format exposes the request as a two-way stream of typed input and output events. The core runs plugins in registration order, allowing them to choose a provider, filter or wrap either stream, make additional calls, return a response, or refuse the request. A provider format then opens the upstream connection. If the client and provider use the same format and no plugin changes the payload, the original bytes and protocol-specific fields can pass through unchanged. When formats differ, they translate through shared types for messages, tool calls, results, streams, and usage. This stream model can represent both one-shot HTTP requests and long-lived bidirectional sessions. The gateway is open source at  https://github.com/respanai/respan-gateway  under the MIT or Apache-2.0 license. You don't need to use Respan's hosted platform and can run it directly on your local machine. Build it from source, add your provider keys, and swap the base URL in a supported client. You can keep using the API your client already speaks. It's still pre-alpha. We make money from our hosted platform ( https://www.respan.ai/pricing ), which runs the gateway for you with native observability and evals, along with unified billing. If you’re building routing, tools, filtering, observability, or security for agents, we'd love to see it as a plugin. PLUGINS.md in the repo explains how to write one and links to the plugins we’ve created so far. Turning that into an ecosystem is basically our roadmap, and we welcome you to contribute your own plugins. We'd love to answer any questions and hear your feedback!  https://github.com/respanai/respan-gateway

title: Show HN: Breadcrumb, record everything on your mac + context manager for AI
author: jv22222
story_text: Hi HN, I'm Justin. Breadcrumb records everything you do on your Mac (screen + meetings + AI transcripts + what you and your AI decided) and turns it into memory your AI can search. It's local and encrypted. You can also teach it rules by talking to it and it makes sure the right rules turn up in the right context. Works with Claude Code / Codex / Cursor / opencode. All of this is exposed to your AI as 30+ MCP tools (here's the definitions):  https://innerloop.works/breadcrumb/mcp  I started it in June because I wanted to understand what was going on with my AI dev work. Then it just kept growing as I jammed on it 10 hours a day for 3 months. I started by recording every screen so I could jump back to a moment and see what I'd been doing with the AI. Then I added MCP so the AI could search it. Then time tracking. Then meetings with transcripts and timestamped screenshots. After that I started feeding the data back in. At first it was just a few relevant memories in the prompt. Then I started adding rules and rules modules. Then I started recording the AI transcripts and all the other stuff the AI did (subagents, tools etc). I wanted a complete record so I could go back and see what the AI did and why. I found the more data the AI had the more useful it became. One example. I got off a zoom call with the team at the day job and said: "Review the meeting I just had, find all the bugs we discussed, and create JIRA tickets with screenshots." It read the transcript. Found every bug we mentioned, pulled the screens from the screen timeline, spun up my local server, diagnosed each bug, reviewed the code, created 14 tickets in JIRA with diagnosis and likely fixes, attached 12 screenshots as evidence, and created a nice Slack message to send to my colleagues. I never built a workflow for any of that. Claude had the meeting record, Breadcrumb tools, and rules I'd accumulated. It basically chained the steps together itself. My favorite thing about the system is observability of my own work as an AI developer. I can trace a bug all the way back to the first thing I said (or the first thing the AI did) that caused it. Then I can add a rule so it doesn't happen again. Anyway, my working system is simply Claude Desktop + Breadcrumb + Markdown. I find I don't need anything else. It's local software for one person. Local models for transcription and diarization. Data encrypted with SQLCipher and a passphrase. You can exclude any apps, websites, words and phrases. Breadcrumb itself only makes one network call which is a daily update check. (but of course your AI will use it and that is local or cloud depending on what you use). It runs cool about 12% of one core on average (M series mac has 8+). You can set it to just save OCR text or to save screenshots. If just OCR it's about 12mb day (a lot of telemetry, indexing etc). If you record screenshots on meetings it's about 120mb/hour (1 every 2 secs). It can also record screenshots of everything that's heavy at about 160mb/day. It does local classification/naming with ollama with Gemma 3 4B (2.5 GB). It's 100% free. There's no account you can just download and start using it. I'll monetize it via E2EE cloud sync and team sync. It's open beta. Just one developer working on it. Requires 16GB+ M Series Mac. Thanks for reading!  https://innerloop.works/breadcrumb  (homepage)  https://innerloop.works/breadcrumb/download  (direct download)  https://innerloop.works/breadcrumb/mcp  (mcp definition)

title: Launch HN: Consus (YC F24) – LLM gateway for companies handling sensitive data
author: ericmags
story_text:
Hey Hacker News! I'm Eric, the founder of Consus. We route all AI requests to ITAR restricted and controlled unclassified information (CUI) compliant infrastructure.
Consus itself satisfies ITAR restrictions, and we recently completed our FedRAMP equivalency audit against the 410 FedRAMP High controls. FedRAMP High is the U.S. government’s strictest security baseline for cloud services handling sensitive unclassified data. A breach of this data could cause severe or catastrophic harm. Achieving FedRAMP equivalency, or authorization, is required before processing CUI information. Demo:  https://youtu.be/6MYxJe6P4oY  Aerospace and defense is experiencing rapid growth. Unfortunately, most companies are struggling to use AI because of necessary data protections & compliance risk. These companies can move even faster if they could use the AI tools that most other industries take for granted. I spent most of my career prior to Consus in aerospace & defense. I launched national security payloads at SpaceX, and was an early employee at Castelion. I’ve watched first hand how compliance red-tape makes it difficult for companies to adopt new technologies and trust vendors that touch their sensitive data. For example, I worked with a satellite manufacturer that doesn’t allow any AI tools, even for non-sensitive work. Even as AI has become extremely useful over the past 9-12 months, I was surprised by how many aerospace & defense companies refused to touch it. They could see how it could be helpful, but they were scared about model providers training on their data, violating an ITAR rule, or risk losing new business because of a failed cyber assessment. These are all rational fears. There were a lot of ways to solve some/all of these problems, but we focused on building a compliant AI inference layer that can "plug" into any AI tool or workflow. Just as OpenRouter integrates with most tools, Consus can connect to tools like ChatGPT or Claude, open source tools including the Pi coding agent or Open WebUI, or integrate with applications built and maintained by individual organizations. Almost no aerospace & defense company lives in all three major GovClouds (AWS, Azure, Google). When I mapped where frontier models can legally run for ITAR and CUI work, each provider had some subset of models, and each model achieved varying levels of compliance. Our customers don’t think in terms of cloud providers. They think about the data controls they require, and the model they want to use.
That is why we built the compliance suffix. Under the hood, every request hits a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint, where keys are verified and policy is enforced before anything touches inference. Every model name must carry a compliance suffix, such as gpt-5.6-sol:fedramp-high or claude-opus-5-5:itar, and any bare model name is rejected. We never proxy to the standard commercial endpoints. Our customers are also able to build an allowlist of models, and assign spend & model restrictions to individual users in the organization. This is all handled through our Consus Portal where teams can manage spend, keys, and policies. A typical question we hear is why not just use Bedrock in AWS GovCloud or Azure Government directly. For small teams, just getting access to these platforms is difficult. For larger organizations, GovCloud lets you inherit some but not all of the controls needed to handle sensitive data. Also, models are split across providers: GPT-5.6 Sol is only available in Azure Government, while Claude Opus 5.5 is served through Bedrock in AWS GovCloud. If you want both, you are standing up and securing two separate government cloud environments. We run all of them behind one endpoint so customers don’t have to pick a cloud, and we handle the compliance work for each one. Given the data sensitivities, Consus does not store any customer data at rest. All prompts and completions stay in memory only for the length of the request and are never logged or written to disk. Zero data retention is strictly enforced both on ourselves and the infrastructure/model providers. We do keep metadata on each request and response for billing and audit purposes. Consus is not self-serve by design. ITAR requires us to know exactly who is on the other end of every key, so we verify every organization and put a contract in place before issuing API keys. We charge our customers a compliance fee starting at $40/mo/seat plus AI tokens at cost. We are actively serving customers, and would love any feedback from security experts, or developers/engineers working in highly regulated industries! References:
API Documentation:  https://gateway.consus.io/overview 
Security & Architecture:  https://gateway.consus.io/security 
Compliance Details:  https://consus.io/compliance

title: Show HN: Graphene – Data analysis toolkit for your coding agent
author: kcmarr
story_text:
My friend and I have worked at a number of BI companies and thought: Can’t a coding agent do most of this now? Almost. They just need a context/semantic layer to ensure query correctness and some kind of artifact for publishing findings and visualizations. We built an open source project called Graphene that provides these tools: - Semantic layer that’s more token-efficient than YAML, more deterministic than Markdown (eg, composable, callable metric macros), with a query API that’s well in-distribution (SQL).
- MDX-like files for dashboards (Markdown with inlined SQL + HTML components for viz with support for CSS and Javascript)
- Connects to popular data warehouses or local DuckDB Your coding agent will build really in-depth reports and can ofc leverage any other skills or context that you've made available to it. We dogfood it inside a monorepo with our website, app source code, planning docs, etc so the agent has access to a ton of context. It’s also nice that the agent can add instrumentation, adjust pipelines and transformations, and add dashboards all in one PR. If you want to try it out, just point your coding agent at  https://github.com/graphene-data/graphene/blob/main/docs/set...  and ask it to set up Graphene. If you don’t have data to play with, you can clone our example project: 1. `git clone < https://github.com/graphene-data/example-flights.git` >
2. `cd example-flights && npm install` Would love any/all feedback!

story_text: Hi HN, Rouler is "rules for your routes". It allows you to steer network traffic across multiple network interfaces on Windows. For example: - Run Tailscale, Mullvad and OpenVPN official clients simultaneously. - Use Rouler to send Slack via the OpenVPN connection, Chrome + an IP range via Tailscale and a torrent client via Mullvad. Rouler is VPN agnostic, so you can "split-tunnel" with anything that sets up a windows network interface. I'm an independent developer from Australia and have been working on Rouler for a bit over a year. It's been a challenging project to say the least, but I'm really happy with how it's turning out. I have spent a great deal of time building and throwing things away, starting over, belting the initial poc into something that I find intuitive... hopefully others do too! I've done all the testing, fixing and improving I can, so now it's open for public beta. I'd love to hear your feedback... and there are some specific points I'm interested in hearing about listed on the Rouler website. Please reply with any questions you might have. Thanks for reading! Brendan p.s. Rouler is "built in Rust" TM ;-) --- On AI (skip if you're sick of hearing about it): Since AI is the hot topic and people are naturally cautious about it, I'll add some quick notes about it, specifically about the driver development as that's the key thing to get right. The driver is hand written and every detail has been poured over many times over. I spent somewhere around 6-9 months manually building and testing just the driver, staring at Dbgview logs, wireshark logs, windows route tables, restarting VM's back to their snapshot and manually copying things across to start again. That's not always the most efficient way of doing things, but it's the way it had to be done. If I had tried to vibe code it Rouler simply wouldn't exist. I did try to lean on AI at times, but it constantly sent me in the wrong direction, told me things weren't possible, tried to take shortcuts and implement poor performing trade-offs. It also loved to hallucinate the windows api. Keep in mind this was around the Opus 4.1 - 4.6 days. Outside of the driver, in user mode land, AI has crept more and more into my workflow. I've had a lot of success utilising the latest models in the app in particular, and I purposefully separated the UI and core logic so I'm able to quickly iterate on the UI. I've also found AI very useful for scripting and refactoring. It has built some great scripts that would've taken me days or weeks to build and fine tune.

title: Show HN: PatchWave - Add static analysis and automerge to Dependabot
author: blimmer
story_text: Hey Hacker News, we're Ben, Josh, and Donnie, co-founders of PatchWave. PatchWave is a GitHub App that combines static analysis and eval'ed agents to analyze and (optionally) auto-merge PRs it deems as safe. If a Dependabot PR breaks your CI build, a fix agent works to get CI passing again. Dependabot PRs suck. Nobody likes dealing with them. Most of the time they go ignored or a senior engineer spends their valuable time dealing with them. Before PatchWave, I ran a freelance business charging clients hourly to do exactly this kind of "keep the lights on" work. Even at our small startup, we'd spend Monday mornings dealing with Dependabot PRs. Having a human-in-the-loop working with an agent on these PRs was time consuming and, often, agents would get lazy and not actually validate how an upstream change affected the codebase. And, as the quantity and severity of CVEs increases, merging security updates quickly becomes increasingly important. PatchWave is a set of specialized agents that uses static analysis tools on context we gather deterministically. 1. We pull the changelog, the code diff between versions, security advisories, and CI results. 2. The agent checks out your code in an isolated sandbox, where it uses structural code search, type checkers and your project's own toolchain to understand how your codebase uses each dependency being updated. Every Dependabot PR gets a report. You can see a few examples (against OSS repos) here:  https://reports.patchwave.ai/alam00000/bentopdf/pull/913  and  https://reports.patchwave.ai/shipshapecode/shepherd/pull/355...  3. If CI fails, we automatically dispatch a fix agent to try to get CI green again. For most PRs, this means updating your code to use a newer API, fixing linting/formatting issues, etc. 4. We have an optional feature that allows auto-merging certain PRs when PatchWave deems them as safe and the PR aligns with your auto-merge policy. Our recommended auto-merge policy is to auto-merge patch/minor/major dev dependencies and patch/minor production dependencies. You can customize this policy or turn auto-merge off entirely. PatchWave will skip auto-merge in a bunch of cases where a human should review. For instance, if provenance changes (e.g., a package that's usually published by GitHub Actions via Trusted Publishing is suddenly published by an API Key), we require human review before merging. Dependabot also instituted an on-by-default 3-day cooldown to reduce the risk of supply chain attacks. If PatchWave makes any changes via a fix agent, we'll always require your review before merge. Currently, PatchWave only works with Dependabot and GitHub. We plan to offer Renovate support in the future. We've eval'ed the agents the most against TypeScript and Ruby, but are always adding to our eval suite to improve accuracy. The fix agent works best with PRs that require modest code changes. For large updates, especially updates that span multiple majors, our fix agent will give up and provide you a remediation plan to help you mitigate. On the privacy/security side of the house, our SOC 2 Type II audit is in progress (see trust.contextbridge.ai). We only run on repos you select, our agents run in a short-lived microVM per run, we use Amazon Bedrock with zero-data-retention, and never train on your code. We're offering 25 free PRs per GitHub org, per month with no credit card required. Additional PRs are billed at about $1/PR, with discounts for higher volume. We also would love to accelerate OSS projects, so reach out to ask about additional free credits. If you hate dealing with Dependabot PRs, we'd love for you to give it a shot and tell us what you think. Josh, Donnie, and I will be around answering any questions and responding to any feedback you have.

title: Took apart Claude Code, then turned it into a free course on harness engineering
author: pauliusztin
story_text:
The fastest way to learn harness engineering? Build Claude Code from scratch. Why harness engineering? LangChain kept the same model and changed only the harness. Their coding agent went from 53% to 67% on Terminal-Bench, a top coding-agent benchmark. From outside the top 30 to the top 5. Same model. Better harness. Over the past few months, I've taken apart Claude Code, OpenCode, and Pi to see how they work under the hood. And you don't need to ship a coding agent for this to pay off. The same foundations power any agent, in e-commerce, finance, or sales. On top of that, people are increasingly realizing they need to build their own harness instead of relying on Claude Code or Codex. Ramp scaling its operations with a custom harness is a perfect example. So I turned what I learned into an in-depth course on harness engineering by building Claude Code from scratch. It's free and open source: 8 articles, 6 videos, and one codebase. It's perfect for people who learn by building. Everything in Python. For full transparency, Modal, Opik, and Kitaru sponsor the course, which lets me keep it 100% free as an independent AI engineer. Here are the 8 steps that I think are core to building and maintaining any harness: 1. Design the harness 
2. Build the bare-bones agent loop  
3. Sandbox it, locally and remotely  
4. Apply 4 essential context engineering techniques
5. Add subagents as a context engineering technique
6. Deploy it headless to the cloud: CLI, webhooks, cron
7. Build benchmarks to measure it  
8. Replay failed runs to debug agents Everything is on GitHub: https://github.com/decodingai-magazine/building-a-coding-agent-from-scratch-course Curious what others here think. Which of these steps has been the hardest to get right in your own agents?

Hey HN, we recently open sourced our Consumer Agent Testing Tool to help teams iterate against proprietary assistants like Muse and Instinct. - Outcomes tracking and comparison

The best way to get started is...to point your coding assistant at the repo and ask it to integrate the tool with your CI or local testing pipeline! Hope it's helpful! title: Show HN: Pi-cowboy – use Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode as subagents
author: suoloordi
story_text:
pi-cowboy is an agent orchestrator for Pi( https://pi.dev ) and Herdr( https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr ). Break large jobs into focused subtasks, hand them off to background agents running in parallel, and consolidate the results when they finish. Each agent runs in an isolated copy-on-write Git work-tree, minimising disk overhead. pi-cowboy can orchestrate foreign harnesses too, including Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and more. Feature highlights: - Foreign harnesses: 
  pi-cowboy agents can run in Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pig and Pi-Bolt, as well as Pi. This gives you great flexibility in choosing how to spend your tokens. Running out of Codex usage? Switch your pi-cowboy harness to OpenCode, select one of its free models, and let it handle the rest.
  Pig and Pi-Bolt are pi variants that are more efficient, with a lower memory footprint and faster performance than pi. Because pi-cowboy is designed to run multiple agents in parallel, having a lower per-agent footprint is crucial. It prevents your machine from running out of resources and lets you have higher concurrency without choking your system. - Concurrency limits: 
  You can configure concurrency limits at every level. Running a local model with limited resources? If a simple task already takes hours to complete, the last thing you want is to overload your machine by running too many of them at once. Set concurrency limits for that model specifically to keep resource usage under control. You can install it on Pi as a package:     pi install npm:pi-cowboy #(requires `herdr` 0.8+)

Code has become extremely cheap to produce, if you have a 5x claude subscription, you can produce or at least try to produce any piece of software you want. But this also means it is getting easier to copy a product, put it on public GitHub and announce you've killed the paid version. Being open source shouldn't give you a pass for shipping slop. If you are calling your tool a replacement for something people pay for, show how it compares. In the past week, each time I opened X, I kept seeing ads about a new open source code review tool claiming to be the "CodeRabbit killer". I have used CodeRabbit in the past and it definitely has its shortcomings, but if you're claiming you've killed a product, there needs to be evidence. I saw the advertisement so many times that I decided to evaluate how the product actually performs, it also gave me an excuse to add review capabilities into my own open source tool called shadowclone which helps me manage my agent skills and ensure that regardless of the harness or model I use, agents consistently follow my engineering preferences. I ran an eval using Greptile, OpenQodex (the open source tool I wanted to evaluate), and my own implementation of a code reviewer in shadowclone, which is basically a code review skill, a local reviewer and a Github bot that can review on the cloud. So i built a simulated city to explore that. it has AI residents that live there with stats like hunger, energy, and money. each resident has its own ai agent, and it has one shared list where agents write down what everyone wants and then work on our behalf to make it happen. that could mean delivering food, giving rides, or finding jobs, relationships, apartments, customers and almost anything else. honestly, the city works much better than I expected, and you can watch some surprisingly advanced interactions unfold between people and agents through the list on the right side. all the conversations and actions are real, everything happens with each person managed by llm with minimal context, just to live like us and context of stats. A simple example:
A restaurant tells its agent, find me customers so the agent writes to the list, "Salina restaurant in SF, selling burgers from 8:00 to 10:00, i want customers" 
A delivery guy tells his agent when he wakes up, "I want to work in delivery now. find me jobs. status: free"
A person at home tells their agent "i want to eat burger. order for me from salina" the person's agent acts as the middleman and searches the list for salina, it finds their item and sees the way to connect with them and contact. the person's agent and the restaurant agent close the deal, and then the restaurant agent looks for available delivery guys in the list and speaks with his agent to come pick it up. ai, instead of software with rules, can figure out the best route and path on the spot. all we need is to align all agents to one shared data source, so billions of agents will update it and maintain it in the most sophisticated smart way no algorithm will ever be able to do. that’s it. i hope it inspires you as much as it inspires me

title: GitHub can f..k you and you are forced to love it. or live with it...
author: anonymous_frust
story_text: In January, Hytale launched in alpha. The owner said: “We officialy support mod” and “As long as the code isnt obfuscated you can decompile it.” Those were his words. I was on the official Discord, among thousands of players wanting to create servers and mods. Everyone wanted to move fast. I saw an opportunity. A huge wave I could surf. So I decompiled the server JAR and started creating comprehensive modding documentation. Three sleepless nights. Two more days. Twenty coffees. My reverse-engineering skills, boosted by AI, working overtime. Finally, it was ready. I published it on GitHub and shared it with the community. Developers thanked me. Two people joined the project. Then I woke up on Sunday morning. Account suspended. Both collaborators? Suspended too. GitHub said my account had been suspended for violating the rules. No specific rule. No explanation. I’m an introspective person. I can connect the dots. All three collaborators suspended after working on the same documentation project—we know what triggered this. What GitHub has never explained is WHY that work warranted suspending our entire accounts. The game’s owner explicitly said we could decompile unobfuscated code. If GitHub had a concern about permission, why not contact the studio? Why were other documentation efforts still available while ours resulted in three account suspensions? The repository was hosted under a separate organization. Our personal accounts were attached to it. But if one organization or repository was the problem, why block three entire accounts, including unrelated projects? We also wondered whether a competitor had reported us. That remains speculation. I don’t know whether the suspensions were automated. But when nobody explains the decision, you’re left guessing. And before anyone tells me to contact support: I HAVE. I followed GitHub’s official appeal process. I sent appeals and emails. I even emailed the game’s official studio asking for help. Neither side answered. From January through September, I waited. It’s October now. Still no account. Still no way to retrieve all my repositories. Since that day, I host a fucking Gitea instance on a private VPS. I no longer trust cloud platforms with so many customers that your life, your life’s work, and your history stop mattering—unless you’re Elon Musk. I have local clones of some repositories. Not all of them. But the loss goes beyond source code. My GitHub account was a witness to years of my life as a developer. Projects, commits, dates, experiments. Thousands of hours of work, long before ChatGPT and the current wave of vibe coding. Today, people can look at what you build and casually dismiss it with “AI did that.” My history was right there. Years of commits showing that I was already building things before any of this existed. That history could speak for itself. Now I’m supposed to start over, looking like just another account created during the AI boom? “Create a new account” doesn’t restore a professional history. And the worst part is the data retention. As far as I can tell, my account still exists. The work is still there. I just can’t access it or extract it. It feels like they’re holding a part of my life hostage. We’re encouraged to publish, push our work to the cloud, and trust it to survive a dead computer. Then the platform suspends your account, locks you out of unrelated work, and leaves you waiting for nine months after you follow its own appeal process. How is this acceptable? If there was a problem with the documentation, identify it. Explain the rule. Answer the appeal. But what possible justification is there for keeping years of unrelated repositories inaccessible? I’ve already spent nine months trying the official channels. I want my work back. P.S. I’m not giving my name. If they care about their customers, they’ll find me. Or not…

title: Show HN: RDST – A local agent that watches Postgres/MySQL for query regressions
author: gvsg
story_text:
We noticed during the course of many many years of DBA related work that fixes to database issues and queries are always reactive. An entire database can fall over extremely quickly when an unbounded query grows without warning. Traditionally, DBAs hear complaints of slowness and follow a methodical process: 
- manually browse pg_stats or other database related performance internal tables 
- see which queries are slowest
- figure out what indexes are missing
- figure out which indexes are actually bad and slowing down writes
- painstakingly implement a fix In the age of cheap intelligence, we decided that there is no reason we can’t have an always-on agent that is designed to do this job for you.  Databases need something or someone that is always watching with a massive amount of contextual understanding to be able to take quick actions.  We’ve watched the alternative play out repeatedly. One of our users’s checkout page went from loading instantly to taking 11 seconds in a single night with no code change.  How? Well somehow their order table grew by 40M rows because BI team had injected historical data and suddenly postgres started doing full table scans. Sometimes routine operations have unintended results and can easily destroy your database. We wanted to catch these kinds of regressions instantly. So we built RDST. RDST is a desktop agent that runs on your PC and connects to PostgreSQL / MYSQL (read only) and compares every query against its own performance every minute. Every expensive query is automatically EXPLAIN ANALYZED, stripped of PII and sent to U.S. based frontier or open model providers to analyze which indexes are missing, how the query could be rewritten, and provides the fix.  We then run a classifier model (JEV) to decide if you should be notified (is this standard behavior for this particular query?), and the full history of the query performance is kept for years.  RDST also keeps track of your entire database health in general, and recommends more fixes than simply bad queries. Since it runs locally we can keep the database credentials stored in your OS Keychain (RDST never keeps them in its own storage layer), and the connection goes straight to your database (using a jump host or SSH tunnel for private connections). You can read more about how we handle data especially as it pertains to LLM use here.  https://readyset.io/docs/readyset-ai/rdst/desktop/privacy  We really want feedback from the community from people running Postgres and MySQL in production. We are giving inference away completely for free. Just as a reminder, RDST will NOT run any updates or indexes against your database at this time.  We are considering a fully autonomous auto-pilot mode in the future, but for now we are leaving the actual fixes in your hands. Let us know what you think!

title: Ask HN: Is this the beginning of the end of open source?
author: potamic
story_text: If you're following the photopea incident, I'm sure you'd concur that the writing was on the wall. It's an inevitable outcome of the rise of AI in software dev. Any project that sees a semblance of success will be cloned overnight many times over and will find itself competing with its own copies. We saw glimpses of a similar situation in the past when large cloud platforms cloned popular softwares in a not a very dissimilar manner. This led to the creation of "source available" as an alternative to open source that gained some traction of its own. But since this mostly affected a few large players, open source by and itself was large unaffected still supported by large volumes of individuals driven by passion, motivated towards their craft. The concept of open source is itself something of an anomaly not seen in any other industry or at any other time in history. Partly fueled by an individual's desire to exhibit original work, and partly supported by the fact that code needs someone of an equal to work with, it still allowed authors to reap a net benefit while giving out their IP for free. LLMs have turned that picture over completely. It's not only trivial to derive, for all purposes, an exact copy of the IP while obscuring the source, it's also possible to maintain and operate the IP with a relatively low bar of expertise. But the other inconspicuous problem brought about by LLMs is that can you even claim original work any more? When no one believes that you wrote it yourself, what motivation remains to continue publishing as open source? With no net benefit to revealing your IP, will we see a revival to closed source distribution again?

title: Show HN: Vibivibi – End-to-end encrypted sharing of Coding Agent sessions
author: hyluo
story_text:
Hi HN, I'm Hongyin. I built Vibivibi ( https://vibivibi.com ) because I kept
starting a coding agent session on my laptop and wanting to continue it on a server, or hand it to a colleague. I want an easier way to do it but won’t trust anyone hosting my traces who promises they won’t sell it (market price per coding trace is $50 to $100). What Vibivibi does: a small CLI, `vibi`, finds the sessions your coding agents
keep locally (Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenCode, Pi), encrypts one on your
machine and uploads it. On another machine `vibi pull` puts it back where
the agent expects it, so `claude --resume <id>` just continues. `vibi push`
can also send a session to someone else by email. Our service cannot read session content. Each user has a key pair made on
their first machine; the private key reaches the server only wrapped with
a key derived from an encryption password that never leaves the user's
machines. Every session version is encrypted with its own random key,
which is then wrapped for each recipient (X25519, HKDF, AES-256-GCM).
The server sees account emails, public keys, machine names, sizes,
timestamps, who sent what to whom, and an optional plain-text label. Sending to someone who doesn't have an account yet works too: the
sender's client makes a key pair on their behalf, locks it with a random
12-character passphrase, and shows the sender that passphrase to pass on
out of band. When the recipient signs up and enrolls a machine, their
client unlocks it locally and re-keys the session to their own key. The client is open source (Apache-2.0):
 https://github.com/subconscious-systems/vibi-cli 
The crypto and the schemas of everything the client sends live in one
package, so the claims above can be checked against the code. It ships
as a single executable, no Node or npm needed:
`curl -fsSL  https://vibivibi.com/install.sh  | sh`, or build it yourself.
The server (Next.js on Vercel, Postgres, blob storage) is not open source. Pricing: free for 200 MB of encrypted storage and unlimited sends; Pro is
$8/month for 20 GB; Team is $15/seat with an admin view and a
"send only inside the team" policy. Honest limitations:
- There is no password recovery. Forget the encryption password and the
  key, and everything encrypted for it, is gone. I'd like to hear where the threat model falls short, and which agents or
workflows you'd want supported next.

So I let that idea rattle around in my skull for a while — and eventually it bounced up against the memory of Ck (Curses-based Tk). Anybody remember that? I liked Tcl/Tk and [incr Tcl] and it had always stuck in my head how great an idea it was to have something along the lines of CLIM for regular terminals as well as GUI. So anyway, I stumbled upon the open-source CLIM2 source still maintained by Franz, and the wheels commenced to turn. Oh yeah, and my very first programming environment had been Turbo Pascal. That integrated debugger was really something. And y'know, it all started to come together as an idea about modernizing CLIM and modifying Portable Hemlock to run on top of it — and integrating a Debugger with conditional breakpoints and Step In/Step Out/Step Over, CLIM presentations, Inspector... And in years past, I'd have just dreamed about it. But the past three years have been crazy. GPT4 was the first time I seriously tried to build things with an LLM. And I've been pushing the LLMs as far as they would go to build my intuition mainly. But up until this year they've been mostly crap. I used "Build Common Lisp" as my north star because the Dietz ANSI tests seemed like a nearly perfect product specification. Long story short: I threw away 7 attempts before I won ANSI —  https://gitlab.com/patchwork1-ai/whateverlisp  — and while I was waiting for Claude and Codex to grovel through ANSI I was trying my hand at my grand idea of Turbo Lisp. Side note: my high score on ANSI is 21,916/21,925 passing (99.96%); 21,925 executed; 9 failing.  And those 9?  Yeah I don't think you could pass those without failing 30+ other ones. So anyway — It’s called *Turbo Lisp* (based on SBCL). It brings together a Listener, debugger, object inspector, conditional breakpoints + stepper, and Zeta—a variant of Portable Hemlock that uses WhateverCLIM as its front-end. On macOS, it uses native AppKit UI through *Chattanooga, a Lisp/Objective-C bridge I built*. It also runs in the terminal through *Oak Ridge, my Lisp port of Ratatui*. Both use *WhateverCLIM*, which is the CLIM2 code from Franz plus my own modernization, including * presentations* : displayed Lisp objects you can click and inspect. *v0.2.1 patch release* is available for Apple Silicon Macs, Intel Macs, and Linux x86-64. The Mac builds currently require macOS 26. I’m especially interested in hearing: * Does it install and start properly on your machine?

title: Show HN: Gauge CLI – Open-Source Hillclimbing for Agent Experience
author: 0x63_Problems
story_text:
Hi HN! We're releasing an open-source CLI for hillclimbing Agent Experience. That means optimizing your agent-facing surfaces (Skills, CLIs, SDKs, and docs) so that your users' coding agents can easily use your product. Pointing your own agent at the repo is enough to get started.  https://github.com/gauge-sh/gauge-cli  We've found that power users generally want to hand a CLI/MCP to their agents and get started from the terminal. They rarely want to log in and use the web UI themselves. We think developer tools must be agent-friendly to remain relevant. Here are some common findings that Gauge identifies: - agents get confused with CLI/SDK behavior and start source diving
- interactive commands block agents
- agents use deprecated/old CLI commands
- agents don't use Skills when you'd expect
- agents confidently assert limitations that don't exist
- inconsistent terminology confuses agents
- agents can't figure out how commands fit together into a workflow Locally, the Gauge CLI uses Docker containers to run agent harnesses (you can bring your own subscriptions). It finds where agents get confused or stuck and tests changes using your pre-release artifacts (Skills/CLI etc). We normalize events from Claude Code, Codex, Pi and OpenCode into standardized transcripts, and store them locally, alongside structured information in SQLite so that your agent can easily analyze the data. This enables automatic hillclimbing toward a great Agent Experience. We also offer hosted compute that enables more features, built on our custom Gateway (for credential brokering and transparent, per-session response rewriting). Hosted compute enables many more concurrent sessions, easier collaboration with teammates, a GitHub App for PR reviews, sessions with logged-in MCPs/APIs, and most importantly it lets you close your laptop while the sessions actually run. You don't need a Gauge account to run the full loop end-to-end though. We expect that local execution with the CLI is enough to find and fix several agent experience issues in a typical project. You'll be able to validate fixes for these issues locally, before publishing new versions (we inject pre-release Skills and code artifacts into the sessions). We would love your feedback!

title: Wiki-driven development: coding agents update a wiki for you, you set direction
author: wek
story_text:
My team has been working in a way we are calling calling wiki-driven development, where the wiki is written for the human, not the agent and the human uses primarily the wiki to set direction for the agent. This is different from Karparthy's LLm I'm curious whether others do something like it. Once I run several coding agents at a time, I get overwhelmed and disorganized. Every session makes decisions and raises questions, and I can't reread the transcripts. CLAUDE.md and agent memory help the agent, but they don't give me a place to see what is going on and decide. The problem gets worse with a team. So, I have the agents write a wiki, and they write it for me. As they work, they record only what is significant: decisions with who made them, when, and the option we passed over; open questions with an owner; and a short summary of where each area stands. I ask it to focus on the big picture, strategy, key architectural or business decisions. In more detail:
1. Agents do the work and update the pages it affects with what is significant: key decisions, key strategic points, open questions, and a summary of where things stand.
2. I read the wiki to understand the big picture: the key points, where we are, and what still needs to be decided. It is short enough to read.
3. I think and decide there: I settle a question, change a decision, lay out some more strategy points, or rewrite a page to say where I want to go.
4. The next session builds from the page I changed. Karpathy's LLM Wiki idea is related, but it compiles sources you collect into a knowledge base that keeps getting richer. His goal is completeness for research. Our approach is minimalistic: the pages distill way down from the agents' sessions, hold only what is significant, and exist only so I can think and decide. Spec-driven development has you write the spec up front for the agent to implement. Here the agent writes the wiki based on all the valuable detail that are in my session prompts and its response and I edit the wiki, so the document keeps up with the agents work and my job is thinking, organizing, deciding, direction. Here are some things I have learned doing this:
- Organization is key for me as the human. I make the agent make a nice visual html with clickable links marketecture or architecture or business model canvas as the top page and navigate from there. I have it keep each page a page long so I actually am motivated to read stuff. 
- Have the decisions record the rejected options, so when someone brings a question back, the reasoning is available. We are constantly revisiting decisions as we work and learn and so this is very helpful.
- The agent wants to write everything down. The criteria I give it is to only record what it would need to get back to where we are right now in terms of strategy, decisions, implementation.  Its not that much. You can do the same with a CLAUDE.md that tells the agent what to record, and work in markdown files or Obsidian or Notion. We got so into this that we turned it into a free, MIT-licensed plugin for Claude Code and Codex that keeps the wiki as markdown files in your repo and lets you see the wiki in your browser locally: https://github.com/nimbalyst/nimbalyst-wiki. Do you work in this way? If so, what other things should we be doing and how have you made it work well?
