title: Show HN: Singularity – memory that makes coding agents cheaper on repeat work
author: luvmakin
story_text:
Coding agents start every session from zero. Ask Claude Code for a change like one it made last week and it reads the same files again, falls into the same test traps again, and you pay for all of it again. Singularity learns from your finished sessions (change committed, tests passing): where each kind of change goes in this repo, how it gets checked, and the mistakes made along the way. When the next task starts, a hook hands the agent the workflows that fit, pointed at the code as it is today. Picking them is plain text matching with no model call. It stores where to edit, never the code itself. Results, medians of 3–4 runs per side, hidden tests decide pass/fail, every run passed. On excalidraw: - A long task with four changes, all of kinds memory had learned: 1.9M → 423k tokens, $0.81 → $0.30, 28.5 → 9.5 turns. - The same kind of task, but two of the four changes were bugs it had never seen: 39% fewer tokens, 38% lower cost. The unseen bugs cost the same with or without memory. - Where it doesn't help: small tasks in validator.js and one-off bug fixes. The difference there is about zero, within noise. Each measurement was written down before it was run. The plans and results are in the repo. Caveats: 3–4 runs per side, mostly one repo. Only Claude Code sessions are learned from; Codex, Gemini CLI and Droid get the hand-over through their hooks. Learning uses your Claude account (about $0.25 a round, capped at $1 a day, and only if you opt in). Everything is stored locally in ~/.singularity. Install (Windows PowerShell and more options in the README):     curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pandacover/singularity/main/install.sh | sh
  
I'd love to hear where it breaks on your repos, and what memory should carry for one-off work like bug fixes.

title: Why the Creators of AI Do Not Understand Their Own Creations
author: borissunik
story_text:
Just citations. Dario Amodei (CEO of Anthropic, 2025):  "People outside the field are often surprised and alarmed to learn that we do not understand how our own AI creations work. This lack of understanding is essentially unprecedented in the history of technology."  MIT Technology Review:  "Despite all the stunning success, nobody really knows how — or why — it works."  Yoshua Bengio (Turing Award laureate, 2024):  "If we continue as before, we are driving against the wall. Or at least we are driving into a fog, without knowing whether there is a wall."  Mathematician Roman Vershynin (UC Irvine), in a recent interview —  "We advanced to the wall and hit it."  So why did AI research hit the wall? The answer is not hard to find, and most people in the field know it, even if they prefer not to say it loudly. The point is that all training data used by AI is secondary, while the primary source is the human being. Every text, every image, every pattern a neural network absorbs — all of it was created by humans. A neural network does not discover the laws of the world; it only finds regularities in what has already been created by human intelligence. So if we want to understand how AI forms knowledge, we must first understand how humans form knowledge. But this pretty obvious idea was never materialized because of the historical failure of all attempts to build a working, mathematically correct model of knowledge. The story started in the 19th century and continued until the end of the 20th. Tens of theories of information, hundreds of books, thousands of articles in dozens of journals — and nothing practically working came out of it. This however does not mean no adequate theory exists. It is there since the late 2000s, but it is still completely unknown to the scientific community. This occurs for a purely ideological reason because this theory builds its formalizations on concepts borrowed from mainstream programming languages and so completely ignores mathematics. For the major journals devoted to AI and information theory that is a taboo. I spent years trying to publish it. The answer was always the same:  "Add the mathematical justification, and then we will take a look."  When I contacted established researchers directly, the answer was either silence or:  "Yes, you have an original idea, but we are not interested."  I stopped trying fifteen years ago. My hope is that now the theory might have a chance, because it addresses exactly the problems that the current conceptual apparatus cannot solve. The Theory of Meaningful Information (TMI) expands the conceptual framework of the most expressive programming language, which is C++, by adding capabilities for creating standard narrative (non-executable) texts that constitute the primary form of any human language. In TMI, information is defined as the value of a variable used in some algorithm. This works for a bit in a computer, a state of a neuron, a pressed button, a written letter. It applies to a bacterium, a program, a neural network, and a human. The theory introduces Information Capable Entities (ICE) and traces their evolution from the simplest biological ICE — a cell — to complex technical devices and the human being, who is modeled as an object controlled by a biocomputer (the brain). It offers a complete algorithm of human knowledge formation, from the simplest perceptions to the most complex concepts. It contains the theory of intelligence, covering both natural and artificial intelligence, and the theory of a universal representation language. A short description of TMI and a link to the complete work: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23403895 Boris Sunik,
independent researcher

title: Ask HN: Is there any defense against LLM-based reverse engineering?
author: semidror
story_text: Recent news headlines [1] about LLM-based reverse engineering make it seem that anyone with a monthly subscription is capable of translating any executable into an equivalent source code representation. If this is true, then how can one guard against having their source code essentially unveiled with the correct semantic meaning of the underlying algorithms by someone with an extremely low amount of effort? I bet that using obfuscators would still not be enough. I'm distinguishing between recreating the source code of your software vs vibe coding an inexact clone without knowing your source code (which is not exactly reverse engineering). Example: Imagine it would be possible to faithfully recreate the source code of the firmware running on a foreign military device, even with correct semantic meaning of variables, functions and of the whole algorithm. On the other hand, vibe coding a clone would require that you know the underlying algorithm (or at least that you have a high-level idea of how does it work), which you don't have for such device. Does it mean that companies like Denuvo are now out of business (assuming anything can be reverse engineered with the correct semantic meaning)? [1] https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50028275

story_text: Hi everyone, This started as an exploration into harnesses and locally hostable LLMs (the kind that uses less power than a small electric heater), and I used it as an opportunity to retool. I've tried popular ones like Cline, Claude Code, and Pi, but wanted a different UX and integrated sandboxes. It feels like a microcosm of my day job: define and delegate tasks, organize using kanban, then review deliverables. And it also feels like the time I used to spend coding is now spent in code review with the agent, so I tried to optimize the UX to make review feel nicer. Now I can jot down an idea, start the task, and at some point down the trail: get a notification* that either clarification is needed, a decision needs to be made, or the code is ready for review. I've been having a good time with this. To build MIKE, I exclusively used locally hostable LLMs (from Google, Meta, Qwen, Poolside, and DeepSeek) hosted with llama.cpp on my machines at home (Strix Halo and a 5090) to "compile" the code. title: Show HN: Cryptex Vault – A password manager designed to outlive its creator
author: Bl4cksmith
story_text:
Hello everyone! About four years ago, a password manager I've used and depended on has been acquired and soon after, it was shut down. If anyone remembers MYKI, it was a password manager that stood out at the time.
It didn't require an email address and a password for registration and it synchronized credentials peer-to-peer. It was quite handy so a couple of my friends and I got hooked, and were using it up until the last day it was online. The thing was, I didn't want to change password managers to other options available at the time, none felt right - I wanted to stay.. So I did what any sensible engineer would do 4 years ago and I wrote my own. I moved all my credentials there as soon as I had a first version ready. It was ugly (God knows I had UI/UX skills to learn), but it worked. Soon after, the same friends that were using MYKI switched over to using Cryptex Vault. I get why, we had the same P2P synchronization across devices, it was simple and didn't try to be the most-feature complete application out there - it did the job.
That was an exciting moment.
So exciting, in fact, that I've posted to HN to tell people about it. At the time, I had a weird  thing  for decentralization so I called it a "Fully Decentralized Password Manager". Three years go by, I keep maintaining the project, with no real intention of proper marketing or polishing. At one point I checked the usage and figured out that a handful of people (and their families) were still using Cryptex Vault as their password manager. Three months ago, I left my comfy job as lead software engineer at a local company to dedicate time to a company I called Cryptex Industries. Polished Cryptex Vault, cleaned it up, made it open source, started providing Docker images for self-hosting and included some of the features I've only used internally (ssh-agents).
That way Cryptex Industries need not remain operational for users to have a path to continued use! To make the project commercially viable, I started offering managed services through the Online Services plan. By using Online Services you remove the operational burden of self-hosting and infrastructure maintenance from yourself while still getting the same benefits: Managed backup storage, synchronization between devices, sharing, ssh-agents, device management. It is convenience, not access to core features.
The core application is free and you can use it with no subscriptions of any kind, whatsoever. It's P2P synchronized, with industry-standard crypto choices including post-quantum primitives for synchronization -  https://www.cryptex-vault.com/docs/cryptography 
It has importers for popular password managers, along with autofill for chromium browsers (firefox is a todo, yell and I'll get on it).
As for the platforms, there is a web app, an android application and an ssh-agent for linux (will put it up on AUR when they open up registrations again). Feel free to try it out (there is a 14-day trial for managed services!), self-host it or break it. I would appreciate your thoughts on this and I wish you a nice friday!

title: Show HN: TowerPanic – a family party game on a small FastAPI realtime engine
author: ms209495
story_text:
I want to show you the game I created recently and tell you whole the story/experience - including backend/latency/scalability. You can try it quickly without an account - I created game demo rooms (EU/US/JP) - links below - just be aware that anyone with a link can access join the game. Let's start with short description of the game itself: This is the TowerPanic game - you are standing on one of four towers, during each round some of towers crack, and some of these lean, and finally one of these colapse - you need to watch out to not be on the failing one.
It's a multiplayer game for whole family.
This can be also used as an icebreaking game - for people in any age.
The game is safe for children - no violence, no strangers, no chat, no ads.
Parent creates an account (free 14-day trial, then a paid pass) and starts the game - others join using a QR code or a link. Behind the game there is an interesting backend engine - I willdescribe it in a moment. Let's start with the history of this whole project:
- I was playing with asyncio and fastapi
- As an exercise I created a reliable chat application (multiple rooms, in each room each user can reliably broadcast a message to all other users)
- I extracted communication to separate layer - creating network/application layer interfaces - 'reliable client' interface for client and 'state machine' interface for the service on server.
- With these interfaces - I was able to create other service - an 'sgame' (simple game). With verified interfaces and created services (chat, sgame) I was able to ask AI to generate other tools/games - I was impressed by these results
- the games/tools worked well - I deployed them on a remote server - I was surprised that the latency was very good - almost everything worked smoothly I tested the tools and games with my children and one of the game was really great.
I decided to make this game public - I chose 'TowerPanic' name for it. I prepared an account/payment server for this game (as a separate FastAPI application).
This was very good choice:
- the game servers keep rooms only in memory - nothing persistent (rooms have expiration date)
- the account server keeps all persistent data (it uses database) Because of this split I was able to figure out how to upgrade and scale frontend and backend independently - without significantly impacting users. I optimized the communication layer - so that it works in finite memory - only finite number of recent messages is kept, and I sent a full service snapshot (full state) to the lagging clients. The backend process (FastAPI/python) is limited by python GIL (only one core can be utilized) - to utilize all server cores I used HAProxy with consistent hashing to distribute rooms - so that users can be redirected to proper backend process. I tested how many rooms a single server can handle - it handles hundreds of active rooms in parallel with no significant latency drop. Before making it public I noticed that latency in other region of world might be higher and this could influence UX - I confirmed this using artificial delay on my remote server. I decided to deploy the application in three regions - EU, US, JP - to ensure low latency (below 150ms) in most of the world.
The room is created in region closest to the user (best latency from the browser to backend). I needed also to prepare some legal documents (terms, privacy, refunds) - thanks to AI this was much easier.
I'm a backend engineer, frontend/UI/UX were designed by me but code was generated by AI. To summerize all this work:

title: Show HN: Craig – A TUI for running parallel coding agents

title: Show HN: Rashomon – An independent execution record for AI coding agents
author: rganupa
story_text:
I have been working on Rashomon, an open-source execution recorder for AI coding agents. The basic idea is that the agent transcript is not ground truth. Rashomon keeps its own record of what happened and compares it against the agent’s account. For Claude Code, it records things like: * shell commands, exit codes, and whether they may have written files
* tool calls and outcomes
* test commands and their outcomes
* subagent lifecycle and ordering
* timestamps and parent/child relationships
* keyed digests of command/tool inputs and working directories It builds a timeline from these events. It does not store prompts, responses, file contents, or tool output. For example, it now detects patterns like: `test fails → only test files change → same test passes` and: `test command fails → same command passes → no corresponding file edit` These can indicate that an agent changed a test instead of fixing the underlying issue. Rashomon currently runs as a Claude Code plugin or through the CLI. CLI: `rashomon watch` then: `rashomon report` Plugin: `/rashomon:report` There are still edge cases around cwd, git state, test-selection arguments, generated files, retries, and parallel execution. I would be interested in feedback from people building agents on what execution signals you would want Rashomon to capture or correlate. GitHub:  https://github.com/altrace-dev-role/rashomon

title: Show HN: Railcode – Secure cloud for internal software
author: yakkomajuri
story_text: Hey HN, Yakko here from Railcode. Railcode is like an internal Vercel for your company. We built it after speaking to dozens of engineering leaders at various companies where employees were given access to Claude Code or Codex and started to build little tools (apps, agents) locally, but then struggled to share it with coworkers securely. Typical scenarios are: 1. Employees can't share what they've built because of internal policies 2. Agents find the path of least resistance and deploy things on e.g. Vercel, leading to a sprawl of software that's a nightmare to manage (disjointed auth or no auth, API keys handled insecurely, no centralized management, etc.) 3. Companies set up templates to ensure some standardization but still require engineers in the loop to review and deploy code Neither of these options felt great, so we built Railcode to be the place to deploy and manage internal software inside a company, ensuring projects are deployed securely, follow the same patterns, and can be easily managed from one place. The goal is to unblock users to deploy and share what they've built while removing the burden on Engineering/DevOps to review and manage it all. How we do this: - Company auth in front of everything that's deployed - Permissioned connectors to access data instead of shared API keys - Infrastructure building blocks that make it easy to store data or use an LLM but allows admins to oversee everything (via a simple SDK) - Centralized audit logs - Unified design system (optional) - Role-based access control with granular permissions that can be inherited by the projects themselves The platform is built to be really low friction for agents and to not require folks changing their workflows. We support static frontends and serverless JS functions for the backend, meaning Tanstack, Hono, Vite, React, etc will all work. Even Next.js with OpenNext though that has some quirks :D Projects run locally and everything Railcode-specific comes from an optional SDK. We ship a skill and a CLI and that's all you need to build and deploy projects or have agents manage configuration. Keen to hear feedback!  https://railcode.dev/

story_text: I didn't like that Claude and codex effectively have the ability to do anything they want on my laptop and my local network - we've all read the horror stories of files accidentally being deleted - and while their permission classifier is getting better, it still requires a lot of trust. So I built Airlock for macOS which runs your agent in a virtual machine, and it will tell you exactly what it's run and what's changed before you bring anything back to your project. You can limit internet access to specific hosts, or block it altogether. It even works with Xcode projects (iOS and macOS developers rejoice). Technically you can run any command with Airlock - not just AI agents (`airlock run -- somecommand`). It's free, requires no account, and has no tracking or analytics. I'm hoping Apple will approve it for Mac App Store distribution, but in the meantime you can download it directly from the website or using Homebrew.

title: Show HN: Fantastic Canvas

story_text: Fantastic is my own harness. It runs on an Erlang-like, OS-like meta-runtime instead of agent loops or agent graphs. I believe this is the right design for an AI runtime: it puts humans, AI agents and tools on equal footing. It will grow into a convenient multi-OS runtime that can do what other AI libraries and harnesses do. For now it’s a technical demo with two modes: a CLI coder, and a spatial canvas that’s very handy for a lot of everyday work. I think the canvas mode is the kind of software we’ll all be using in the 2030s. I don’t have a name for it yet, so for now let’s call it “emergent software”. The idea is that you build, run and engineer your own systems visually, with help from AI, inside your own dynamic interface that you build for yourself. It’s a lot of fun, especially for multimedia projects. For example, in a canvas project I’m still working on, a third-party AI agent generates UI and agents: it builds a control panel for making a Manim animation, and a viewport for a Blender video built from the Manim animation’s guidelines. title: Show HN: shadowclone, skills learned from your coding agent corrections
author: theonly1me
story_text: shadowclone reads the coding-agent sessions already on your disk, finds where you corrected the agent and turns those corrections into skills your agents load next time. It supports Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Pi, and Antigravity. Every capture source is off by default and has its own consent setting. Why I'm building it? I use multiple harnesses and agents, I extensively use Claud Code and Codex, but I also use Cursor and Antigravity every now and then. I didn't want to have to teach every harness or model the things I taught the other ones between my last session and the current one. I also cannot have my personal rules and preferences in all the repositories I work on because my collaborators may have varying levels of trust with AI and their own preferences. shadowclone helps me build and improve trust with my agents so I can give them more autonomy while running multiple sessions in parallel. --- Who is this for? If you only use Claude or Codex or any one of these, you may not need the shadowclone CLI and the harness and agent you use might already be sufficient. But, if you are like me and work across harnesses and agents, shadowclone will help you avoid repeating your preferences each time. --- Built-in skills and skill builds shadowclone is also great for someone who is just now adopting AI into their coding workflows because it ships with several skills that they can use to customize their agent's behavior. They can equip all the skills, or just some of them, they'll see the "personality" their agent gets from equipping those skills from the `shadowclone wizard`. --- Setup is extremely easy, just ask your Claude Code, or Codex, or another agent - "Set up shadowclone:  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/theonly1me/shadowclone/mai... " --- Privacy shadowclone is free and open source, it uses the MIT license. It doesn't have a subscription, or a server. It just uses your existing agent subscription i.e. Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Antigravity, or even your local model via Pi. You can explicitly disable sources, it also redacts any and all sensitive information it uses for learning. --- PR reviews and Cloud bots It can review PRs with the `shadowclone review` command, it ships a guided review skill that will perform a deep review of your code (or someone else's) and produce an HTML document you can annotate, add comments to and submit so your agent can stage a draft review on the PR you are reviewing. --- Evals I performed several evals, I won't describe them here, all of them are available in the repository -  https://github.com/theonly1me/shadowclone/tree/main/evals  --- Comparison to other tools? title: Show HN: Treesum – Replace MS Excel/Project with a Code Editor
author: mallahan
story_text: # Intro The goal of this software is to make it easy to get the plan that's in your head onto the page. Start with the outline then add details. Then more details. Then numbers: costs, time, quantities. Then organize and categorize with #tags. All the sums, graphs and pivot table functionality happens automatically in the Calcs, Timeline, Stats views. And everything looks nice without you having to format it. Currently, it's all local, saved in your browser. Save your plan permanently by downloading the '.tsum' file. Open (upload) the '.tsum' to start working again. Everything happens in the browser. The files are stored where ever you like. The '.tsum' file is just text - human and AI readable. Use it to plan anything. We hope it works like your brain does - by organizing things in trees. # Story This software is entirely vibe-coded. It had to be - none of my developer friends would help me out. The front end JS on this app is too complex for a part time developer like myself. I've had this idea for a while and was only able to bring it to life because of AI. It may not gain traction, but at least I can put it out there, use it myself, or stop thinking about it altogether. It's amazing to see it and actually use it - to know if my idea was good or not, at least for me. And I'm actually happy with it and have been using it. If you have thoughts about the idea, feel free to let me know. I'm open to suggestions for improvement. # Disclaimer This tool is mainly intended to help with project planning. But it can be used for any data that looks more like a tree than a table. Creating a quote or estimate for one-off projects is my favorite use case. The varying structure of costs across lumber, electrical, concrete and labor fits well. Obviously, it doesn't replace all the many things Excel can do. It tries to improve on MS Project by making it easier to get your schedule on the page by coding into an editor instead of poking at menus in a GUI. It is still a proof of concept at this point, not a bullet-proof software package. If there's interest, it will be developed further. For now, it's good enough for me. # Roadmap I want this software to be the Excalidraw of Excel: free, simple, browser-based and fun to use. There are great things that Excalidraw does that would require servers and more costs. These features could be turned into a paid product if there is interest. So, if you're interested, please let me know: treesum.app (at) gmail.com. # Thanks HN This project would not have been possible with out AI. But also not without HN. Reading HN nearly every work day really shapes how to think about software and presenting it to people - especially for someone who is not a full-time developer. It's a great community and I've happily been a member since (at least) 2013.

title: Show HN: Loudwalk – Review your Anki deck out loud on a walk
author: cracadumi
story_text: Hey HN, Loudwalk ( https://loudwalk.com/?from=hn ) is an app I built for myself to review my Anki flashcards out loud on a walk, and am excited to share today. Anki has changed my life and is probably the best habit I've managed to stick with. Apart from helping at my tech day-job and remembering random things I find interesting (relatives' birthdays, quotes, poetry), it allowed me to become conversational in Russian in 2 years and complete the first year of a French university degree in Art History - all while working full-time as CTO and co-founder at my company. I have an average memory at best, and it is crazy what Anki unlocks with consistency. Recently I've been exploring how interacting with LLMs by voice can help me spend less time at a screen and more time active and outdoors, for two main reasons: - wanting to be more active/healthy as I'm in my mid-thirties and starting to get back pain - just had a newborn and spend a lot of time carrying him or doing chores around the house Most of my time sitting at my desk is spent waiting for coding agents and reviewing Anki cards. After building Notiferry ( https://notiferry.com/ ) to forward macOS notifications to my iPhone, the next obvious move was Loudwalk: an LLM asks your card questions, listens to your spoken answer, and grades it. Voice reviews give a cadence I don't have on screen, cutting my daily review time in half (from 90 minutes to 45), and walking while reviewing helps both memorization and mood. Time simply doesn't have the same flavor staring at a monitor vs walking in nature or holding your baby. What Loudwalk does: - Import your decks with full history and media from Anki (and export back to Anki with no lock-in; includes a starter deck and CSV import if you don't use Anki yet) - Start a voice review from any deck (works with Siri so your phone stays in your pocket) - Spoken grading + "deep dives": if you stumble on a card or want context, ask out loud to start a live conversation on the subject, with live web fact-checking when dates or connections matter. Say "next" to return to your queue - Question rewording: rephrases questions so you memorize the concept, not the exact card wording - Phonetic grading + deterministic timing: on-device STT mangles proper nouns, so the LLM grades phonetically/semantically against your card's answer, while response-time caps (Again/Hard/Good/Easy) are applied deterministically in code - On-device speech recognition; grading and deep dives use OpenAI models (a mix of GPT-6 Luna and Sol + GPT-Live-1) It runs on iPhone (iOS 26) and Apple silicon Mac (macOS 26). No Android or Windows. I haven't planned to open-source it for now as I'm seeing if it can support me working on it long-term. Visual reviews (Anki-style) are free forever; voice reviews require a subscription ($9.99/mo) after a 7-day trial (no account or credit card required). Sync across Mac and iPhone uses append-only JSONL review logs in your own iCloud Drive - no server in the sync path, and visual reviews + sync + export work offline forever. I switched to Loudwalk over 3 months ago (>3k spoken reviews) with first-class support for English and French, plus a CLI so coding agents can add cards at the end of a study session. Happy to answer any questions about the app or spaced repetition!

title: Show HN: Benchmarks of continual learning model trained for a month on a laptop
author: volotat
story_text:
A month ago, I shared mini-AGI, an experiment in training a byte-level, continually learning language model from scratch on a single 8 GB laptop GPU (an RTX 3070).
To recap the setup briefly: it completely decouples model size from VRAM by paging experts to and from an NVMe drive (currently 397 experts / 1.26B total parameters on disk, with only 32 resident / ~109M active in 5.1 GB of VRAM). It trains on a single stream at batch 1, with the attention/embedding trunk learning rate dampened to 0.1x to mitigate catastrophic forgetting. The training is still going and went only through ~35% of the training corpus selected at the beginning of the run (about 8GB in total). Here is the current status: 1. enwik9 (First 10^9 bytes of English Wikipedia):       Model               Params   Data Read       Cost     enwik9 (bits/byte) ↓

    Llama-3.2-1B        1.23B    36 TB (9T tok)  ~$900k   0.68
    Chinchilla 1B       1.00B    5.6 TB          ~$68k    0.90
    GPT-2 XL            1.56B    40 GB           ~$43k    1.07
    GPT-2 Large         0.77B    40 GB           ~$21k    1.12
    mini-AGI (online)   1.26B    2.8 GB          ~$56     1.14
    GPT-2 Medium        0.35B    40 GB           ~$10k    1.17
    mini-AGI (dynamic)  1.26B    2.8 GB          ~$56     1.23
    mini-AGI (frozen)   1.26B    2.8 GB          ~$56     1.29
    GPT-2 Small         0.12B    40 GB           ~$3k     1.33

  
2. PG19 (100 Project Gutenberg books, 41 MB test split):       Model               Params   Trained On        Cost    PG19 (bits/byte) ↓

    MambaByte-972M       0.97B   75 GB (PG19)      ~$4k    0.883
    MegaByte-1B          1.02B   80 GB (PG19)      ~$1.6k  1.000
    Transformer-320M     0.32B   80 GB (PG19)      ~$1.6k  1.057
    mini-AGI (online)    1.26B   2.8 GB (0 PG19)   ~$56    1.447
    mini-AGI (frozen)    1.26B   2.8 GB (0 PG19)   ~$56    1.995

    The published models were trained on PG19's own training books, 75 to 80 GB of them, and are scored on more books like those. mini-AGI has never been trained on PG19 and has read no Victorian novels, so for it these books are completely out of its domain.

  
There are more details in the repository. The most important part is a difference between "frozen" and "online" attempts where we allow the model to specialize on the task as it goes through the evaluation dataset. Clearly showcasing the power of continual learning regime simply unavailable for any other typical LLM. Full methodology, and replication code is in the repo:
 https://github.com/volotat/mini-AGI  Intermediate weights snapshot on Hugging Face:
 https://huggingface.co/Volotat/mini-AGI-undertrained

title: Show HN: Laya guard – a local check before your coding agent runs a command
author: ayaan0209
story_text: HN, this is my first Show HN post, and I'm really nervous, I'm Ayaan, a Frontend Developer. laya-guard is a local check that occurs before any coding agent tool call, deciding whether to approve, send for review, or block the call. When Jev was released, I was curious as to how I could use it, and I quickly discovered Laya which is an open-source 322M model that functions almost identically but runs on a laptop's CPU in under 100ms, as the check is local, there won't be a chance of 3rd parties seeing your commands, directories, or tokens, and there's no charge per call, I often work in Korean, and most of the guardrails I've seen have not evaluated Korean at all, hence why I've implemented it as well. Regex policies catch known dangerous patterns before even reaching models, any command that is blocked is never seen by models, commands like ls, git status, and npm test will skip the model altogether, unless they have pipes, chaining, redirects, -exec flags, or sensitive paths, everything else is sent to the model for processing, once you have the model downloaded, it makes decisions from a fixed set of outcomes with no API key or request needed for any external service, there are also hooks for 11 different agents including Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and many more. And Also a local dashboard where you can see all decision and why it was made and install the hook for each agent, it doesn't save the commands themeslves. In my tests with AgentDojo, it blocked 25/27 attacks, and allowed 92/97 harmless tasks, it correctly identified 64/66 commands I made. After the Reddit post, people have found some issues with it: Adding a comment at the end of a command would fool the model to not block the command. The model only read the first 4,000 characters, so it could be spammed with junk to the beginning to bypass the check, this would send dangerous commands like curl to review. "curl" repeated 40,000 times caused one regex to run for 48 seconds, timing out the hook and running the command. All 3 issues have already been fixed, somebody also pointed out that if the server was down, commands ran without any check, now it asks you first, or blocks the command if the agent can't ask Please note that this is not a tool to check if the code written is correct, it's a tool to prevent agents from running dangerous commands.

title: Show HN: Trustmux – Async tmux from your phone, now in Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora
author: dustinkirkland
story_text:
I'm Dustin Kirkland, author of Byobu. I recently flew to Australia and kept nudging my Claude, Codex, and Bash jobs along back home from somewhere over the Pacific, at 700ms of latency. That's what Trustmux is for: secure, asynchronous access to your tmux or Byobu sessions from your phone. I first posted this in June and since then there have been many point releases, lots of new features and testing, and a growing base of users. It's now packaged in Ubuntu 26.10, Debian, Fedora, and Chainguard OS. Why not SSH, Mosh, or Claude Mobile? - SSH/Mosh: a live, synchronous connection is brutal on a phone. Latency and WiFi-to-cellular handoffs make it laggy and fragile.
- Claude Mobile: great for Claude, but I wanted access to whatever is running in my tmux session: shells, Claude, other code assistants. Trustmux is async by design. Connect, look, type a command, disconnect, with no fragile connection state to babysit. Security: TLS with real certificates, end to end. Uses Tailscale (cert provisioning via tailscale serve, no port forwarding) optionally, bind to your own network address, or bring your own or self-signed certs. Two security experts reviewed the design and I implemented their recommendations. More scrutiny is very welcome. Quick start:     trustmux enable
  trustmux start
  trustmux pair   # shows a QR code if qrencode is installed
  
Open the URL on your phone, enter the 6-digit code, and add it to your home screen. It's a PWA, so there's no app store. Install: apt, dnf, pip install trustmux, or brew tap dustinkirkland/trustmux && brew install trustmux Under the hood: Python, libtmux, WebSockets, Tailscale, and no polling. The UI shell is cached for offline use. Part of Byobu, GPLv3. Trustmux isn't affiliated with the tmux project.  https://trustmux.dev

story_text:
This package is designed to solve two problems: 1. Frontier models like Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Astra 6.0 and Sol 6.1 all make errors and bugs that can be found by another model (even a much smaller model like Luna). 2. In what is supposed to be a long development run, for example against a plan, models will decide to stop before they are finished, when there is obviously more work to do, or to ask a question they already should know the answer to. ReviewerAgent blocks git commits and sends them to another agent that reviews the staged files and either allows the commit or returns a list of issues to fix. StopContinue evaluates every agent stop and determines if it still has work to do or if it is asking a question that it has the answer to already. In either of those cases, it prompts the agent to keep working and specifies next steps or answers to questions, based on the current plan document and chat history. The system works for and is tested on Claude Code and Codex as the developer harness, and either of those or any other model, through Pi, as the reviewer. I've developed it over the last 4 months or so and used it daily over that period. Take a look if it sounds useful. It's been tested on MacOS and Linux (Ubuntu), and has agent assisted install, update, and removal scripts, for convenience. Stats: Over four months of daily use of the system while developing it (from late June til today), reviewerAgent (usually a GPT Luna model) gated 3,877 commits, running about 7,600 reviews in total, so about half of those commits were rejected at least once. The coding agent (Fable or Opus) almost never disagreed with the reviewer's judgements: over the last month, for example, it pushed back on just 3 of 693 rejections. Each rejection listed an average of two required fixes and most rejected commits were accepted after a second round (90% within five attempts). Rejection rates increased with commit size: only 23% of code commits under 50 lines were sent back, but 72% of those over 1,000 lines were initially rejected. Here's an example of a bug that it caught last month for me. More examples in the README: The Fable 5.1 developer agent wrote a wrapper script that runs a set of R validation checks against a freshly loaded database and records whether each one passed. (One of two required fixes shown.) REQUIRED FIXES (blocking)     2.  docs/database-phase-loader/local-load/run_r_checks.sh:4-6 pipes each R check through
      tail without pipefail or explicit status handling, so a failed Rscript can still
      produce a zero exit status and be recorded as successful. Preserve and propagate each
      check's exit status.

  
In a shell pipeline the exit status is that of the  last  command, so `Rscript check.R | tail` reports `tail`'s success even when the check fails. The script prints the tail of the failing check's output, exits 0, and records a pass. A broken load would have been certified as validated.

title: Show HN: Nodecode, open-source living agent in Lisp that rewrites itself for you
author: svsairevanth
story_text:
Hi HN, we're Mike and Thom. Agents of the future should only have one tool (the interpreter, ideally a LISP eval), nothing more or less; to interact with the world. Agents remember by writing markdown files. NODECODE remembers by rewriting itself. And that is in itself a new paradigm in working with agents. What if memories, skills, MCPs, provider connectors, tools, etc. all live under the same image as *.lisp files instead of in disarray across random folders? Ask it for something it can’t do, and it writes what it needs into its OWN running image and keeps it even after a restart. (Changes in a LISP image have significantly lower ceremony and overhead than in harnesses written in other languages): Small intuitive scenario: > you can't read PDFs. teach yourself.
   (defun read-pdf (path) ...)        ; runs at once, kept
   (read-pdf "invoices/0421.pdf")
   ;; Globex owes $1,240.00, due Oct 24, unpaid. [… rest of PDF content] read-pdf is still there after a restart, in your terminal, and in every other UI clients (Discord, web app, etc.) Technically at a lower level; NODECODE runs as one process in SBCL, a Common Lisp system, and shells attach to it. The model has one tool: it evaluates LISP in the running program. Code is data, so a program can rewrite itself while it runs. What the model defines runs at once and is kept, one file per definition, committed with git, loaded at every start. Why LISP now? Current SOTA models have reached an optimum point in how they efficiently work with LISP, though not as fluently as Python. Still, we believe AGI will understand ANY language (past/present/future) by understanding the crux of any given language, and not through excessive and expensive pretraining scheme. Why LISP in general? We believe LISP is the current language that communicates to the world with the least bandwidth. Why another LISP agent? The LISP harnesses we found are hard to use unless you already know the language itself, and so we had this idea of simplifying and condensing the UX to be user friendly for the masses, while leveraging the power of LISP. Code as data is what lets an agent change itself, and that shouldn't need a LISP hacker to run. NODECODE is our first step toward putting it on everyone's PC and mobile. You ask in plain words, the model writes LISP, and you get briefed in natural language; that is how it should be. Extensions? Code as data also suits extensions. We see NODECODE as a living agent organism. To us, it feels very much alive, and so this brings us to the Cells system. A Cell is a folder that teaches NODECODE something new: a chat room it can live in (e.g Discord, Telegram, Slack, etc. - Yes we made Cells for channels to have it act as a very capable personal agent), a skill, a memory, MCPs, new tools, etc. Install one from our Cell hub or ask it to write a custom, personalized one. Either way it is more code the agent can read and change. Your terminal, a browser tab, your phone and bots in Discord, Telegram and Slack all attach to that SAME gateway process, so a tool it writes in one is there in ALL of them. Over time it becomes yours and it is continuously evolving; the organism within it; NODECODE. MIT License.  https://github.com/nodecode-ai/nodecode

title: New Python security updates explicitly block the eMudhra certificates by SPKI
author: zahlman
story_text:
Thanks to Python core developer (and Python 3.14 and 3.15 release manager) Hugo van Kemenade on the main Python discussion forums for the heads-up[0]. The patch[1] is contributed by Christian Heimes (with Claude assistance), former core developer who spearheaded the discussion on the bug tracker[2] and quickly affirmed the seriousness of the problem in the discussion thread (post 2, which corrected my mistaken assumption that pip would ignore its bundled `certifi` certificates as long as `truststore` was able to find system certificates). Blocking is implemented by a pretty straightforward loop, memcmp'ing against the hard-coded `unsigned char _distrusted_spki[][SHA256_DIGEST_LENGTH]`. As explained in comments: * This is an extraordinary measure and last line of defense.  Removing trust is
 * primarily the job of the platform root store. This list only blocks keys while
 * that update is still propagating to the OS, container images, or root CAs
 * bundled in Python packages.  The threshold for adding an entry is very high. There's also an amusing workaround for security scanners that might trip on the  tests  included in the source release. From the code comment: > The distrusted test material… lives in a password-protected zip so it doesn't trip security scanners that cannot tell internal test fixtures from production secrets and flag any certificate or private key they find.  It is encrypted, not merely zipped, because such scanners read inside plain archives.  The password is fixed, public, and not a secret. What might that non-secret password be, you ask? Well, this is Python, so of course:     DISTRUSTED_ZIP_CHOSEN_KNIGHT = 'Brave Sir Robin'

title: Can an AI learn what you like, rather than just what you've searched for?
author: kartless
story_text:
I'm a writer who was pondering the problems with getting my work discovered and realized that current search/recommendation engines don't go very deep. So I thought about ways to address this. I was obviously mostly interested in books, so I worked on that first. I'd noticed LLMs are capable of pretty solid textual anaylsis these days, so I wondered if you could use that to generate good recommendations. So I sat down with an LLM- ChatGPT, Luna, for the curious- and spent about two hours explaining, in datail, my literary tastes- going into specifics like what sort of plot structure, characters, and humor I like, not just genre/specific titles. The experiment demonstrated surprisingly strong results (though admittedly with a very small sample size)- the five recommendations I asked for were all ones that I hadn't heard of, as well as books that I would actually read. Further, I provided the LLM with a list of several books I had read and asked it to guess whether I would have liked them and why. The LLM successfully did so. Just proof of concept, but intriguing. The problem with this, of course, is that most people wouldn't sit down with an LLM for an extended period of time to discuss literature. So I decided to build a small prototype of an app that might be able to do that. The prototype is very simple- first, there are two types of information it saves- a persistent preference profile for the user, and user conversations. Then I built conversational functions to call an LLM to have conversations with the user to extract preference information. The interesting thing to me is that this isn't just using an LLM to make recommendations- it's using one to analyze conversations over time, develop a persistent, evolving preference model for a specific user and then use that model to guide an LLM on a search for recommendations. A few things occurred to me. First, the conversations and user profile DO NOT need to live on a central server- they can be stored locally by the user (or in a cloud of their choice). Second, it seems like the user data could potentially be minimized and pseudonymized before being sent to the LLM, though I lack the technical expertise to know what is realistic here. Third, if the LLM is conducting any searches, this would seem to make it possible to provide search services with less information about the user and their preferences (I'm not positive about this, so please do correct me if I'm wrong). Finally, books are just one of the things you could use this for- it could technically be done for just about anything, at least in theory. I experimented with this process several times, and received encouraging results. What I don't know is- Is this architecture novel? 
Does it work on things other than books?
Am I an outlier in how well I articulate my preferences?
Am I wrong about the potential benefits to privacy?
Would people use this? If the search results are as qualitatively higher for others as it was for me, I think they probably would, but I just don't know. The reason I'm posting this is because I am a writer, not a software engineer. I don't really have a strong interest in developing this and could bring very little to the table on the technical side. But it seems like a neat use of the more advanced LLMs we have these days. I don't really know if the idea is novel (not in each part- every bit of the pieces has been done before- but as a whole). I'm in the process of documenting the prototype and experiments- I'd be curious to hear if I am completely barking up the wrong tree or if this could actually be a cool new way to conduct searches. I'm not posting this as a business proposition- it's just not my jam. If anyone wants to take the idea and run with it, I'd love to see what you do with it.

Hi HN!
I’m not a software engineer by trade. My background is in behavioral science and human-computer interaction, but I wanted to solve a specific problem I found when applying for jobs which is the logical test. They are booooring, easy to cheat on if you really want to and provides very limited information about people. I built this prototype from scratch sing AI to bring my idea to life.
So now I've been working on this side project for a Cognitive Adaption Engine (CAT/KAT in swedish) for about three weeks. Many pre-employment screening tests i've done use a static item bank and are very liberal with the time allowed on each question, making it easy for Vision LLMs or bots to beat. 
I wanted to see if I could build a fast, client-side engine (JS/SVG) that combats this problem by measuring certain biometric cognitive signatures like "switch cost" (how long it takes for your brain to re-adjust when logical rules change) and "post error-slowing".

If you use an LLM, the constant latencies gets punished with a lower score. If they use a script, the complete lack of natural human variance will be picked up on.
I am currently trying to calibrate a baseline and need high-aptitude users to stress-test it and to provide more data. It also makes it very fast to complete. Everything runs 100% locally in your browser and since I did use AI, I would love your feedback on how the architecture holds up and the technical approach to anti-cheating or anything that comes to mind on this topic. title: Show HN: Enso Method – agent skills for building software for someone else
author: dwkerwin
story_text: The Enso Method is a new set of AI skills for Claude Code and Codex which I've open sourced on GitHub predominantly for developers who build for someone else who is making the product/business calls. I've been using AI to write basically 100% of my code since late 2024, back in the Sonnet 3.5 days, when it barely worked and there were few people doing this and very little support for this way of developing. I stubbornly thought this was going to be the future and came up with a methodology for making it work, before "AI skills" were even a thing. Since then I've continued to refine the method and I just recently published it as open source. The method focuses on requirements (PRD, TDD) up front, and has skills that autonomously refine the requirements, declaring assumptions that should be validated by stakeholders.  It doesn't expect you to be a solo founder or that whoever is at the keyboard directing Claude or Codex to be the product owner and business decider in addition to being the developer.  I think most of us sit in the seat where we develop for someone else who decides. And if AI is all about velocity, then if we have to slow down to get product owners to review and decide, that puts a serious damper on the efficiency everyone expects from AI development. So a defining attribute of the Enso Method is, when it reviews the requirements prior to implementation, it asks what questions/gaps there are and it tries to answer its own questions.  If it can get to 95%+ confidence in the answers, it just rolls with those. If less then it will declare the assumption in an assumptions.md file which gets routed to business stakeholders to review.  In the meantime however we still consider this to be a green light, we can move forward and implement with the assumptions, and if we later hear from the business that the assumption was wrong, we update the requirements and re-implement, because implementation is now cheap, and waiting isn't.

title: Show HN: Lightweight, self-hosted, web analytics app
author: composer42
story_text: Hey everyone! I just wanted to share a little project I have been working on. It's a lightweight, minimal, self-hosted, web analytics app alternative to Google Analytics, Umami, GoatCounter etc. Tldr: Created a self hosted web analytics app that is one binary (docker image available). AI was used to assist. Check it out if you care. I wanted to self host a lightweight web analytics app to see if any of my pages had any visitors, but all of the self hosted apps I found were either way to heavy for what I was looking for, or simply didn’t have a UI/UX I liked. So I just made one myself. The app features a dashboard with multi-site and subdomain support, and some simple filtering on date and visitor details (all EU regulation friendly, so no PIs such as IPs etc). A bit about the process: As I wanted it simple and lightweight, a single executable was the goal. Deciding for the frontend was easy since it doesn’t need SEO or any server side rendering, therefore I chose React with plain CSR (thankfully the DX these days is nice with Vite). The backend was a bit more tricky, since I wanted to have it fast, but also be able to get an MVP out sooner rather than later. The plan was thus two folded; first to do it in Deno to keep everything TypeScript and to implement features fast (it is still my go-to language for prototypes), then to refactor everything to a compiled language (Go or Rust) once I considered the app feature complete. So I started the prototype, but just a couple of days later, the announcement of Deno being sunset came out. As I had already gotten to a point where the backend was mostly functional, I decided to pull the plug early and refactor! The tough decision was Rust vs Go, and Rust ultimately won as I like the DX and how the language looks and writes a wee bit more. So I did what most engineers do in 2026 (looking at you Bun), and I asked my AI for help. Although I consider myself pretty ok with Rust, there are still parts that I haven’t wrapped my head around fully, so as the intention was to get something out fast, I had to bite the bullet. Lastly for the database I wanted something embedded, so SQLite was the natural choice. The final app ended up with a decent ~10mb (down from ~250mb with Deno) which I don’t think is too shabby. Some quick benchmarking on 1 cpu and 2gb RAM told me it could handle ~16.000 incoming analytics requests per second. The bottleneck being the database writer lock (give it more CPU, and it can do better). As this is a hobby project, and I dont expect a peak load of more than maybe 10 a day, I am content with this. I consider this app mostly feature complete, and will use it for the next month before eventually releasing a v1 after fixing whatever bugs that may show themselves. If you think you can improve the app further and want to spend time on it, feel free to make a PR ^^ To sum up the stack: React+Vite+TanStack+Tailwind frontend, Rust+Axum backend and SQLite database; all compiled to one binary of about ~10mb. Disclaimer: Yes, AI has been used for parts of the development, docs and for commit messages, but the code has been reviewed and iterated over by me, a somewhat reasonably sentient human.

title: Show HN: tsv has fast formatters and parsers for Svelte, TypeScript/JS, CSS
author: ryanatkn
story_text: tsv is a set of performance-focused language tools for the Web. Today it ships formatters and parsers for TypeScript/JS, CSS, and Svelte, including a vscode/openvsx extension. JSON and HTML are planned, maybe linting after. The readme has a loose roadmap -  https://github.com/fuzdev/tsv  tsv's benchmarks show how the Web's newer native tools have some performance left on the table. Formatting TypeScript, tsv is more than twice as fast as oxfmt, and is smaller and uses less memory -  https://tsv.fuz.dev/docs/benchmarks  From the site: - formatting TypeScript, tsv is ~2.2x faster than Oxfmt (native), ~36x faster than Prettier (native Rust vs Prettier's JS; ~26x as wasm), and ~7.6x faster than Biome (wasm) - formatting Svelte, tsv is ~79x faster than Prettier (~55x as wasm) and ~10x faster than Biome (wasm) - formatting CSS, tsv is ~3.6x faster than Oxfmt (native), ~111x faster than Prettier (~78x as wasm), and ~12x faster than Biome (wasm) tsv is focused on the Web and Svelte, and doesn't support other nonstandard languages like JSX/TSX and SCSS. This limits possible adoption, but it keeps the tool slim and simple, and there are plenty of other tools that offer a generic language platform - tsv isn't trying to compete with them. Part of my motivation was being tired of slow tools and Svelte's second-class status in this next generation. Before starting the project, I had tried to build on Oxc and Biome, and ran into some discouraging edges. On the benchmarks' language support section, you'll see Oxc doesn't export its CSS parser (recently added, a fork of Raffia -  https://github.com/g-plane/raffia ), and Biome doesn't export its parsers. Also oxfmt doesn't ship wasm to the browser yet, and tsv's smaller footprint is useful there (Biome is 46.9 MB to tsv's 2.7). Parser conformance is as good or better than Oxc, Biome, and swc, except negative parser cases (errors), which are unfinished.  https://tsv.fuz.dev/docs/conformance  The codebase turns 1 year old at the end of the month. It's my first serious AI-generated project, built with Claude Code.  I learned Rust in 2015, built some toys including an arcade action prototype, and followed its development over the years, but this is my first project since. tsv wouldn't exist without LLMs - it requires far too much labor for a side project. tsv leans heavily on Prettier, but doesn't copy it. This is why this production release took almost a year, despite the silly fast coding part. I made some different stylistic choices, more for Svelte than TypeScript, and fixed numerous quirks and bugs and documented them. tsv also takes advantage of Svelte 5's whitespace rules, which further diverged from HTML to trim leading whitespace in tags, fixing longstanding formatting warts -  https://svelte.dev/docs/svelte/v5-migration-guide#Whitespace...  The formatter takes no style config, and instead is hardcoded to Prettier's style with Svelte's config. Supporting Prettier's config would force significant costs on tsv with a JS runtime, so instead I'm keeping the formatters non-configurable instead of making all users pay those costs. Part of these costs can be see in the CLI benchmark (which is a fork of Oxc's official bench-formatter) - when tsv's binary is used directly instead of via Node, the single-repo CLI benchmark runs tsv 1.7x faster using less than half the memory. Next I'm exploring rearchitecting to Zig-inspired data-oriented parsing -  https://mitchellh.com/zig/parser  - which should get tsv closer to Yuku's speed, measured on the site. The vscode extension is `fuzdev.tsv-format` -  https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=fuzdev.t...  - and Open VSX -  https://open-vsx.org/extension/fuzdev/tsv-format  Repo:  https://github.com/fuzdev/tsv

title: Show HN: Stop Claude Code from compacting mid-task
author: LippInc
story_text:
I run long sessions with Claude. For a long time I've had Claude in the middle of some difficult coding task, and then I see the auto-compact message pop up. Every time I wonder if Claude actually picks everything up correctly and nothing is lost. Claude told me 78/82 auto-compactions landed while Claude was working. For a while I couldn't do much. At first I made a skill that would make Claude explicitly save progress throughout long runs. But that didn't fix the core problem and cost more tokens as well. Now that mods came out, I fixed the actual problem. catnap tells Claude at 50% context what the context is and that it should finish what it's working on, write a handoff, and then initialize compaction itself. When Claude finishes its task, catnap compacts, and Claude can then pick up work again. The handoff replaces Claude Code's default summary, so we don't do similar work twice. If Claude for some reason doesn't compact before 60%, it gets a stricter note. And Claude Code's default auto-compact kicks in at 70% as a backstop. The 3 numbers are all settings. After I took on catnap, 0 of 129 naps came mid-task: 98 of them in benchmarks and 31 in my own sessions. The cost is the same as the default auto-compact kicking in at the same point, in tokens and dollars, on 200K and 1M context windows. Compared to the default auto-compaction that kicks in when context is nearly full, catnap used 56% fewer tokens. But lowering the default auto-compact will get you most of the way there as well. I measured memory today as well. Claude worked through tasks one message at a time while 20 instructions and facts were said in the chat, inside long chatty messages, and nowhere else. Asked right after compaction to list them from memory, no file reads: all 20 were listed with catnap and with the default compaction, in every run (15 with catnap, 5 with the default). So in my tests the memory was exactly the same, but catnap got there with a handoff 60% shorter (4.0K tokens against 10K). I was surprised that catnap is actually faster than the default option. This wasn't even one of the reasons I wanted to make this, it just happened. Since Claude writes the handoff in one go instead of the separate summary call the default makes, and the note is shorter, tasks finish sooner: measured end to end, 406 seconds instead of 464. Try it with nothing installed:     npx github:LippInc/catnap
  
It prints how often auto-compact cut in mid-task in your own logs (reads numbers only, sends nothing). Install (needs Claude Code 2.1.287 or later, where mods are on by default):     claude plugin marketplace add LippInc/catnap
  claude plugin install catnap@lippinc
  
Currently Claude Code only, tested on Windows and Linux. The memory test used made-up coding tasks on a 200K window. Some related tools: compact-adviser, handoff-compact, session-pilot and sub-agent-compact. What catnap adds: Claude finishes its piece first, and the numbers on where the cut lands.

title: Show HN: IDE for a general-purpose visual programming language "Pipe"
author: toplinesoftsys
story_text: I'm happy to announce the release of the web-based Pipe IDE, availablle by clicking button "Try Pipe IDE" on website. Pipe IDE requires no account - all data is stored locally in your browser's database, keeping friction to a minimum. ====== Frequently Asked Questions 1. Why now? The need for visual programming has become especially clear now that we're building with AI, which has introduced several serious problems that appear unrelated - yet visual programming addresses all of them at the root: - AI predictability and customization. Instead of relying on one unpredictable, hard-to-customize model - which can only be changed through costly, time-consuming retraining - you can split it into small, specialized, and therefore more predictable agents, then build an explicitly programmed orchestration layer on top to coordinate them. Customization then happens through that orchestration layer, and visual programming is a far more user-friendly way to do it. This shift is already underway - specialized models like TypeSafe's Jev are built for exactly this kind of orchestration. - Cybersecurity. AI makes it far easier for anyone to find and exploit vulnerabilities, so threats are growing. Because Pipe is semantically powerful enough to keep the entire program as a live visual graph in production rather than compiling it into a single opaque artifact, every block in an application stays directly accessible. That access solves two long-standing problems at once: slow patching, by swapping, disabling, or rerouting a faulty block in place instead of waiting on a full CI/CD deployment; and partially-blind monitoring, by tapping the inputs and outputs of any or all blocks directly, so telemetry no longer depends on log statements that may be missing where you need them.The EU Cyber Resilience Act's core demands map directly onto these capabilities - independent confirmation this approach is where regulation is heading. - Code review. AI writes code faster than developers can review it, and leaning on AI to review AI doesn't fix the root problem - that AI can hallucinate too, so human eyes are still required. Visual programming gives those eyes a far clearer representation of the logic to review. AI-introduced errors are already piling up in production code - one study found nearly a quarter survive for months as silent technical debt. 2. Why start with a book instead of building the software first? Most new languages start with an implementation. For visual languages, that software-first path is exactly what traps them in a single domain and keeps them from ever becoming general-purpose. I did the opposite and specified the full language first; the software is what I'm actively building now. It avoids both failure modes. Software-first visual languages get stuck in their first implementation's domain, while purely theoretical ones get buried in complexity - too intricate and incomplete to be practical. Pipe takes the middle ground: well-chosen, practical primitives within a complete, coherent architecture. The book's subtitle says it best - "A Pragmatic Approach to Visual Programming." It rests on seven years of R&D but stays in the practical lane, and the result is a consistent, usable, end-to-end visual language. 3. Do we need to rewrite our existing system in Pipe? To some extent, yes - but the transition is far less disruptive than it sounds: - The migration is gradual - you don't have to discard all existing code at once. You start by wrapping your entire project in a single top-level block. That's the initial step. Then, whenever you're ready, you add a workflow inside that top-level block and distribute the code across the visual blocks of the newly created workflow - and you can keep going, level by level. - You choose how far to go. You can stop subdividing blocks at any point, so it's entirely your decision which parts of the system become visual and which remain as text. - Pipe makes integration easy. It provides a simple bridge for connecting visual blocks to your existing text code. - AI reduces the overhead of going visual. AI can generate diagram layouts from your existing code, update them as the code changes, suggest how to partition logic across blocks, and flag structural issues as your model grows. 4. We tried visual programming before, and it didn't work. Every technology advances in a spiral - it fails several times before its lessons are learned and it finally succeeds. Pipe was built by studying exactly why earlier visual languages fell short. Two lessons in particular shaped it: - A visual language must be both general-purpose and semantically powerful to compete with text. Text-based languages dominate precisely because they have both qualities; any visual language that lacks either will fail. Pipe has both. - The answer isn't to swing between extremes. We tried pure visual programming, it didn't work, so we went back to text-only - which has its own problems, now made obvious by AI. Good engineering doesn't jump between extremes; it finds a synthesis that keeps the strengths of each while minimizing their weaknesses. That's Pipe's core philosophy: it doesn't replace text-based languages - it complements them. In practice, that means the developer decides what goes into visual diagrams and what stays as text.

story_text:
I run my business on four Claude Code agents: Titus, Pheme, Davinci and Metis. They write my newsletter, The AIgent (about 9k subscribers), every day through a drafting and proofreading engine that Pheme checks before scheduling. They also build AI courses, run a pipeline that turns the day's featured repo into a talking-head video of my avatar for Instagram, set up ad deals, and run Meta ads and email funnels with me. Nothing closes until I sign off. Metis posts jobs on a job board and the others claim them.
The hard part wasn't any single task. It was keeping the agents coherent over weeks. Compaction kept dropping the small decisions, and then an agent would redo work I'd already ruled out.
aigent-os is my fix. At a context threshold (80% by default) the agent writes a capsule, a checkpoint file in git, and has to reply with one exact line. Only then does the runner send /clear, wait for a SessionStart receipt proving a fresh session started, and resume. One ack buys at most one clear. If anything is ambiguous it stops at HOLD:clear-stalled-after-ack and doesn't retry. On resume the capsule is reference only, live state wins, and anything the writer couldn't capture is written as Unknown. First run interviews you with three plain questions and makes a first plan. Each agent gets its own memory vault.
Limits, honestly: the public evidence is 11 of 11 cycles on one Windows seat. The runner can still miss a permission dialog (#104), a seat launched from inside another Claude Code session can lose its transcript (#98), and scrolling the seat window sends stray input (#99). v1.1.0 shipped on Sunday.
Try bash install.sh --dry-run, it writes nothing. I'd like to hear where the loop could still double clear or strand a session.

- comment directly on the spec, on a specific area of the image or a timestamp of the video

title: Ask HN: How to organize teams to ship AI-written code?
author: alentred
story_text: Inspired by the discussion in [1], I have an adjacent question: did your team organization and work methods change? In our company we still try to play by the (old) book: backlogs, estimates, iterations, feature teams, PR reviews, etc., but the entire thing leaks everywhere you look. There is no point in many of the old rituals, but it is also not clear how to organize ourselves now. This is different, albeit closely related, from the question of how to adjust as an IC. For example: - In our team, we almost don't see the point in PR reviews anymore, not in the old way anyway. Generated code is always good enough, and in a sense is already reviewed once by the developer who signed off (the topic is discussed in [1]). So, we are now thinking to abandon PRs, or change what we review and how we do it. We are adding more rules for code review agents and to CI. We are also thinking to replace code reviews by "concept reviews" or similar. - Speaking of those, we still try to find the right place and a process for architecture and specifications reviews. They seem to become a new subject of PR reviews in fact, but we are not there yet. - In many places we don't see the need to share the workload and knowledge between multiple developers. Reverting to the model where one developer is responsible for an entire component seems viable again. Although we are naturally worried about BusFactor=1. - Some Agile-inspired practices still work for us, namely iterative development and "deploy when ready". But the development process itself starts to resemble the old-school waterfall-ish one: think everything through, write down your constraints and your specs, design the architecture first, then (re)generate the code at will. I wonder what other practices will go away or get adopted. There are probably more examples, hopefully you get the gist. I am very interested in discussing how do we organize the teams now? What did you try? What works, what doesn't? [1] https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50151036  (Ask HN: How to deal with shipping AI-written code you don't understand?)

title: Show HN: A scroll-through subway ride to show how GLP-1s work in your body
author: mparker123
story_text: I was looking at GLP-1 explanations on the web (full disclosure is that I founded a GLP-1 tracker dashboard) and saw that many had standard text, along with illustrations showing arrows pointing from GLP-1 to a bunch of organs. I didn’t think those sites were particularly memorable or helpful in understanding the actions and side effects. I’m an MD + computer science hybrid with a background in building interactive tools for helping people understand medical concepts, so I decided to build a free scroll-through explainer in the form of a subway ride. The ride is 7 stops, takes about 5-10 minutes, and doesn’t require an account. This was with the assistance of AI, using multiple tools. The process was far from one-shot and with me heavily in the loop for all the different pieces. I still find it tricky to get something medically accurate  and  useful when the details matter. I had built a free set of pages, GLP-1 Field Guides, to help people understand the different GLP-1 related drug classes, and I was able to lean on all of that research and sources to get the details right and to provide authoritative sources for the information presented at each subway stop. I had tried building this starting in February but then paused it for a few months because the models weren’t quite at the point where I could make what I had in my mind’s eye. In the final piece, the different animated elements are drawn in code and change with the scrolling. Here are some of the tools I ended up using: - GPT Image and Nano Banana, both via a custom Claude Code skill I wrote, with my own sketches as the base, for the Field Guide visuals that were important for this piece. Nano Banana for the subway graffiti and the organs - Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS for the conductor’s voice - Suno for the song (ride to the end) - Claude Code with Opus 5.5 to build the site and Codex for code review I am curious if this is a useful format for understanding GLP-1s but happy to answer questions about any of the above.
